THERE S SUNSHINE IN DECEMBER. In winter, when the skies are sad. • And sunshine bright o'er-clouded, And all the blue of sunny days, With cold, gray mists enshrouded, When all the world seems hard and chill, Then sunny days remember; • For though the skies be oft o'ercast : • There's sunshine in December! When sorrow and cold trouble come . . .

To chill thy joy with weeping, And all thy life seems lone and sad, Unblessed, nor worth the keeping— Look up and onward Oro' the mists, And happy days remember; The sad. low clouds Swill clear away, VITI There's sunshine in December!

Sink not, oh heart, look gladly forth! 17' ' Look onward past thy sorrow; pp. Though clouds Co-day enshroud the sky The sun will shine to-morrow; r' Then bear thy sorrows with calm joy, • And in thy heart remember, The future still shall make thee glad Like sunshine in December! •—Cossell's Maga:ine jor December.

NEW YEAR'S EVE. Tho' t' weather's boosth dismal un frosty, Ther's a gret den! o bustle on stur Titer's chaps muffled up. topcooats buttoned, Un wimmin wi' wrappers an fur, 0 full o' good natur, un jolly— Tho' God knows as there's theawsands as grieve—. As they tek sprays o' red-berried holly, Wi' good cheer hooam o' glad New Year's Eve. Ther's fooak ut's bin savin' ther shillin's, Ged o sooarts o' stuff, up un deavrn, They're set on a blow-eawt ut New Year, Un nod to an odd hawf-a-creawn. Wl' gradely-filled baskut on bundle, Th' nwd poss tightly gript into t'kneive, Like "Darby un Joan,' couples trundle, Buyin in, to keep up New Year's Eve. Ther's t' chap as hes won in a raffle, Or bowt th' lucky number th' draw, He's sant rayther thickly fro' t' bottle, Un his greetins are th' noisest or o' ! He maudles, on maks silly bother, Wl' his prize nestled on his cooat sleeve, Un yo' think then "Geese like one another," For yo' will jooalr o' glad New Year's Eve. Ther's lots, rayther pottert for money. On th' keen scent to buy a chep feed; But ineyt sellers stick to ther' figgers, Un to bargainers pay little heed. They know varra weel t' stuff ut's wanted, Un they'll puff, an' do owt, obbut thieve; Doesn't t' butchers ov o' sooarts look daunted, When they ratch t' truth o' good New Year's Eve. 0 sooarts jostle shouthers th' Market— Wiseacres, un sherpers un fiats; Ther's beggars, un "flashers," on dandies Wl' mistletoe sprigs i' ther hats; Un plenty hawf-clammed, ut's beawt money, Think sadly, as they've nowt to cleave. For sitch poor souls ther's vast little honey I' th' prospect o' cowd New Year's Eve. Stroll rea.wnd to them chaps as sell rapnuts. Bi gow ! Dorn'd they wedge id i' price! When they've t' cheek to ax three bob a couple— Or mnoar, iv ther o'er plump on nice. Hares, turkeyA. on ducks gooa up sudden To prices yo'dThardly believe; Hey, th' balance o' profit's a good on, For they warm id o' brisk New Year's Eve. JACK 0' ANN'S.

A physician has discovered that the older a man grows the smaller his brain becomes. This explains why the young men know everything and the old men know nothing. Burke had written a tragedy, which he showed to his friend Fox. Being asked by the latter if Garrick had ever seen it, "No." replied Burke "I have had the folly to write it, but the wit to keep it myself." "Doctor, do you think I shall recover?" "I don't think anything about it, I know it." And pulling a paper out of his pocket be hands it to the patient. "Here are the statistics relative to your case. You vee that one nut of every hundred is cured." "Well?" asks the sick man, nearly frightened to death at the announcement. "Well! you're the hundredth I've treated ; the other ninety-nine I lost. AN UNSATISFACTORY PRYSICIAN.—SeveraI years ago a young doctor named Mabee came out from the East and settled in a small Dakota town to practise his profession. He had a diploma from one of the best medical schools, printed on sheenskin, which he carried around with him in a heavy block-tin tube. He got but little to do; most of the practice was monopolised by a man named Dag- gett, who had been located at the place some time. Daggett did not follow any regularly recognised school cf medicine, but pinned his faith td a ,noultice made on the "hide side of the skin of a black cat,killed in the dark of the moon." Mabee was at last himself taken sick. He got quite low, and finally called in Dr. Daggett. One day, after he had recovered, he was waited on by a committee of citizens, headed by the mayor, who broke the ice by remarking—"Do3., we'uns called on a little p'int which we reckon will he middlin' interestin' to you." "All right—go ahead," replied the young physician. "We noticed that when you got 'perty sick you called in Doc. Daggett to fix you up.' Why, yes, he .came to see me once or twice." Y-a-e-s, we seen he did! Little bit skeered of your own med'cines, we 'low?" "No, sir: but I was too sick to do anything for myself. That's all professional." "It may be perfess'nal. but it won't wash in these diggin's, young man! Here you been tellin' all the time that old Doc. Daggett wa'n't no good, an' pokin' fun at his black catskin poltices, an' saying that mebby he would do fer , cows an' mules, but that he wa'n't quite up to hosses an' persons yet, an' now when yer sick verself the first thing you do is to send for him ! Here you been pourin' yer lin'ment an' condition powders an' one truck an' 'nother down us fer six months but when yer sick yer- self you're mighty glad to go back to the good old catskin! Millions o' bottles of your stuff fer the rest of us, but not a drop fer yerself ! That's the kind of a doe. you be ! We're onto your plan, and as cheerman of a committee of our leadin' ciezens, I want to warn you to move on ! Git right out o' town—a man what da'sn't take his own med'cines can't dose the rest of us, n,ot in this place ! "—DoNta

KING STtPIIEN AND HIS HOSTAGE. A touching incident, which is mentioned in only a few of the school books, is thus related in the Band of Hope Reviem i—After the death of Henry 1. of England (Ist December 1135) a civil war ravaged the country for many years. The kingdom was claimed both by the deceased monarch's nephew, the Earl of Blois, who had been crowned under the title of King Stephen, and by his daughter, the Empress Maud; and many nobles and other powerful men took sides with each party, so that the strife was long and bitter, though in the end the reigning Sovereign got the upper hand. Amongst the barons who had sworn to support Stephen, and to be true to him, was one who bore the title of John the Marshal; this man, on leaving the Royal camp, for his own private reasons, left behind him his little son as a hostage, that is to say, as a pledge of nis own good faith. It was in the year 1152, whilst the King was besieging the town of Newbury, in Berkshire, then in possession of the esemy, that tidings were brought to him how that John the Marshal had proved him- self a traitor, and, with all his forces, had joined Atlaud's army. Great was Stephen's anger; though a good and brave King, and in many respects an admir- able character as a man, he had a fiery temper; and in ' the first heat of his rage at having been so deceived by a man whom he trusted, he gave hasty orders that, since the father was out of his power, the son should suffer, and that his head should be cut off without delay. The followers to whom this cruel order was given, horrified at the idea of murdering an innocent child, andknowing the King's better nature in his calmer moments, con- sulted among themselves how they might save Use boy, and at last sought the aid of a priest who was in the, camp, who by his holy life and his wisdom had gained great influence over the King. The gbod man gladly undertook to do what they asked him, hurried to Stephen's tent, and by his pleadings and rebukes so worked upon the Monarch's feelings that at last he decided to see the little hostage himself before the sentence was carried out. So the boy was brought before the King. When he came- in he went fearlessly up, and having knelt respectfully, stood up and looked smiling into the handsome face—for Stephen was one of the handsomest men in England. He had in his hand a bundle of the flowering stalks of the common plantain, or waybread (Plantago major) ; in many parts of the country the children call these koapes, a name taken from a Danish word meaning a soldier; they have a common game which is played by two—each takes a plaintain stalk, and the players strike each in turn at the one held by the other, trying to cut its head off, and the one who succeeds oftenest has the victory. Looking up in the King's face, the child asked him to play, and, to the surprise of all around, Stephen, touched no play, by the innocence of the request, consented, and tlqi game began. In a little time all the King's kempes were head- less, and the boy was coneuerer; we may well believe that the naturallv good-hearted Sovereign allowed him- self to be overcome without much difficulty. The game being tht,s finished, Stephen took the boy in his arms, and made a solemn vow, before all his courtiers, that from tout day the son af his treacherous enemy should be to him as his own son, should be brought up at his expense, and trained in all that was then thought need- ful for a tentleman to know. He kept his word; and so it came that, in after years, the little hostage grew to be a good and great man, and is still spoken of in history, under his name of William Marshal, Earl of Fembroke, as "the wisest and noblest of the barons."

BY POVERTY NOOK INTO FURTHER STRAITS. A MIGRATION OF THE WOOft*OcK., BY JOHN PBBILB. - The returning sun found us reclining—ft not on a bed of roses, at least upon what, to our grosser natures, was even better—a bed of good edible cockles. Need it be very strongly asserted that these innocent natives suffered the capital penalty, having been found guilty of the crime of being good to eat? With eager active hands we dug the luscious molluscs from the sand and immolated them en the altar of appetite—this being, I guess, the grandiloquent for boiling, eating, and enjoying them exceedingly. The early morning tide had left us high and dry along with the rest of craft in the lake, now lying aground at all possible angles of re- pose. We doft the leathers and the socks, and went to work barelegged and barefooted to earn our breakfasts, which, having earned, we ate, and then the passenger and I " trode a measure." oh the sands. I think " strode " a measure or two might be substituted. Anyway We had a long tramp*over the sands in search of echinus. But "a plague on all technicalities say is the common sea utchin whose prettily-marked shells are so very conitnon on these banks and among the tide-line wrack; sea- worn waifs bereft of their spines, the tenantless tenements of the sea. Their living brothers are to be found in quantities On this bank, ".klEast Hoyle. at the mouth of the lake, Shout opposite the end of the Dove Spit, yhen the tide is out. Well, the passeng,er and I set out and tramped across the sands until we found there was not time to accomplish the task. So we re- turned from our bootless errand, shoeless and in- echinate. East Hoyle is a bank some five miles long, three broad, and twenty-four feet high from low water mark. The channel or lake, even at half-tide, separated the bank from the shore. It used to be a practical channel from the Rock chan- nel to Hilbre Swash. one of the outlets of the Dee. and the western boundary of our bank. On the east we were bounded by vitt of the lake, part of the Rock Channel and the whole of the Horse Ch an- tosl. It thus makes quite an extensive sail to cir- cumnavigate it. Now it was noon, so I turned cook for the nonce—despite the proverb as to the origin of that officer—and turned out a mess—l think that is the proper term -- of potatoes and tinned meat. Despite the manifold demerits of the cook the mess disappeared, and no evil effects fol- lowed. Now the tide was already making outside, and threatened to cut off our communioation with the shore. So Alf and the passenger volunteered to dare the dangers of the deep, and the blistering miseries of the arid sands in search of water and provisions. At last we and the tide were right for essaying the upper exit from the lake. The deep, if by this name you dignify what at best is but a Iriggot through a shoal, is narrow, ahallow, and tortuous, and requires the tentative method for its proper navigation. It is a matter of feeling your way by constant sounding, first on one side, then the other, and when the deepest part has been past "down helm," "bout ship,' and off on the other tack. We managed te scrape clear, although we "smelt the bottom" very often, as was shown by the clouds of sand that we left in our wake. The Red Stones passed, our shoaly difficuNes were 3ver for the time. Let us geologise. The situation is exceedingly suggestive; on either side of us extend long stretches of sand, now covered, though sparsely, with the tide. Now Hilbre Island, -whither we are tending, is an outlier of the Cheshire new Red Sandstone which, , probably, with its sister islets, the,Middle Island and the Little Eye, indicates the former contour of the Cheshire shore. Anyway, Hilbre Island is the westernly limit visible in this neighbourhood of the Lower Tries of Cheshire. Over the Dee, five miles away at Mostyn, coal is worked. This is of interest to Warrington, for, sup- posing the coal of Lancashire and this in North Wales to be bf tha same geologic level, our town and neighbourhood has rich aubterraneous deposits of this mineral blessing. But alas, these blessings, like many others, are out of our. reach. The coal in our dis- trict lies too deep to be profitably worked with the ap- pliances at present at our disposal. But let us hope! The resources of science are not exhausted; nor all the secrets of nature revealed. And, in the meantime, "our universal mother, Dame Nature," by the result of her own operations, has brought up this precious rock within a workable distance of the surface in Lancashire by thrusting.up the flag stones of Billings and Uphol- land on the upheaved flanks of which the coal "crops out," and is workable southward as far as Collins Green, and doubtless runs beneath our feet, then under the Mersey and the Dee to crop out again on the flanks of the Welsh hills near Mostyn. But our thoughts have been underground long enough; it is time they cropt out And surely the beauty of the scenery and the loveliness of the day might well tempt even a hermit from his cell! The clear green of the water is laughing respon- sive to the sun's sweet kiss, and rippling withlthe light touch of the westerly breeze. On our right we had a great and apparently boundless expanse of dancing sunlit water, Liverpool Bay and the Irish Sea; oil our left part of the river Dee with its Cheshire shore. Before us the little red-rocked green tont Island of Hilbre, with its signal station house picked out in vvhita. Then in lessening gradation comes the rabbit haunted Middle Island, and further south the beacon-bearing Little Eye, just large enough to hold a tall mark to warn navigators of approaching danger. Now between these Islets and the shore there lies an almost perfect level of good hard sand. Over these sands, at low leater, pass many visitors, on foot or by trap, to enjoy themselves on the Island. Now in the rock of the Middle Island there ia.a cave —not as big as Keats—but large enough to hold a man, and therefore big enough to be the foundation of a romance, or a tale of smugglery. Well! within the precincts of this cave stiltlinger the echoes of a gallant rescue effected therefrom. The presiding Naiad still sings the praises of the loveliness of the maidens who sought shelter in her cave, and the distinguished valour of the men who sped to their rescue! It was the old " Woodcock " that, like au aquatic Rosinante. carried her owner the skipper, aud his Sancho Panza, Simon, to the rescue of these distressed damsels whom the tyrant; giant Aquarius had confined upon this uninhabited is- land. The boat at the time was lying in the "deep," under the steep and rocky sideof thelargeatisland. Itwas the hour of dine; and we were actively engaged in the 1 duties of the time—we were dining, when it was noticed I that someone was waving a white handkerchief from the Middle Island. A signal of distress, volunteers to the rescue! Now, according te Cervantic precedent, our skipper, whilethe anchor was being weighed and the boat rowed to the spot, ought to have called out in a loud voice: "Re ye not afraid, oh! gentle ladies, and most beauteous princesses. The valiant and renoweedKnight of the Scull: hastens to your succour and will engage the the malignant tyrant who has thus enthralled you, and, with the valour of his single arm, release you from his clutches." I say this might have been said. What was said was to the purpose of getting us to the scene of action as ex- peditiously as possible. It proved to be a party of ladies and gentlemen who had started, rather late for the tide, to cross to the island, and had been caught by the in- coming tide, which reached tho horse's girth ere they found a refuge from the advancing foe upon the Middle Island, in the little cave of which the ladies sought to repair the damage old Neptune had been ungallant enough to do them. The gentlemen were strolling about the rocks, the horse was quietly making the best of things by cropping the scanty herbage untouched by the tide, and the trap was drawn out of harm's way up the rocks. Would we kindly ferry them across to the larger island? We ran the boat on the beach, as near to the cave as possible, and then the skipper and Simon waded out to them, and carried the ladies back into the boat, except the elder one, who said that " being wet, it mattered not being a little wetter," and she waded to the boat. When the males had embarked themselves,we rowed them over to the island, and bade them farewell and fare better next time. But, see! We are clear of Hilbre, and have now the fair expanse of the wide Dee before and armed us. Where the extreme right hand landscape merges into the sea is the Point of Air, with its lighthouse ; and beyond that again the tall and far seen shaft of Prestytyn ; then Mostvn vomiting white yapours,the beae.en-like chimney ef Llannerch-y-mor—our destination—and mist-crowned Flint, all backed by a fine range of mountains. On the left the tamer beauties and the lesser heights of the • ,• with pleas-

Cheshire shore displayed themselves, dotted with pk ant homesteads. With an increasing breeze from the W.N.W.. we sped along merrily through the rising seas. The sails, includ- ing the jib, which we had set at starting from Hilbre, urged the old lady to the top of her speed, and gallantly she responded to the call. Merrily the foam bolls flew by her side! Angrily the sea hissed at the treatment it received, as the dividing stem threw them, white with resentment, carelessly aside. TI-Us went on increasing, ' till we found it, best to take in the jib. Alf struggled with the writhing rebel, and got it dowli (and a wet- ting), but could not get it in hoard. owing to a jam of the outhaul in the heel of the " jibstirk," and pro- bably, also, to the different tutture of the footing afforded by the prancing deck, from that of Scotland (toad. The situation i and sensations are so unlike! Now my friend is quite at home in the water; a queer fish though, mind you! He can swim like a fish, dive like a Kingfisher, and float like—like—let me see—a whale? no not "very like a whale "—something more etherial or aerial—well. a bladder! And yet he objects to old Neptune dousing him in play! Truly an odd fish! but a good fellow. "Youth at the prow, and pleasure at the helm." This we know makes the ship go gaily, but now I had to re- verse this and call the youth from the prow to Palinurate, whilst I went forward to complete the jibstowing. This

done, things resumed their wonted course, but, shocking to say, Mr. Alf has had nothing but evil words to say. of that blameless piece of timber the bowsprit ever since. 'Oh!, how deeply thankful I felt that we had ho ladies r board ; but as it was, a bright half-crown I had in .... pocket showed its displeasure by going black in the face. Meanwhile a black cloud whichlonghad topped the Flint- shire Hills now left them and came towards us accom- panied, as usual, by an increased breeze. This, howeyer, proved to be of the Hombastes Furioso kind, more threat than performance. We carried a whole sail into-Llam nerch-y-mor. . Here we snugged up for the night. band Alf..and I strolled along the shore and among' the ruins of different works—to Mostyn to post a notice of our arrival to the Skipper who was to come with Simon to meet us on the Saturday. After a pleasant walk we got on board and slept like tops, after eating like thrashers. (To be continved.)

div.head: BARON VON GRENTSTEIN.
div.p: BARON VON GRENTSTEIN.
A. TERRIBLE AND THRILLINO CHRISTBAS STORY WITH GHOSTS
AND THINGS. BY LUKE SHARP.
Liberty W. Palladium, ot Chicago, entered the great bortals of the Gruntkein Castle on the Rhine one evening' in September. He never came out again alivelmt! •

Grim old Baron Von Gruntstein sat in the great dining hall of his castle. Be was not in very good humour, for the cook had given warning the week ' before, and the new one showed a: tendency to having the melds behind time. He had been an ,official on the continental railway before he became a c,ookiaad so it seemed the most natural thing in the world for him to say, when the valet came down and said that the Baron was waiting for supper, or dinner, as the case may be, that the meal was two hours late. On this wt.:ikon ther Barer: was drumming with his fingers on the table and using, sotto toes, the most terrible German Imprecations. The trembling menials knew that very soon the storm would break, and that the Baron would begin throwing whatever was handy and portable at them, if the viands did not soon make their appearance. At this awful moment the valet, or the footman, or whatever person whose business it was to make such an announcement, opened the door and said, in A loud voice:

"Herr L. W. Pendulem, of Tchichago." "Palladium, if you please," quietly remarked the owner of the name, as he followed up close at the heels of the servant who announced him; "and the name of that city is pronounced She-caw-go, as doubtless the Baron knows. Good evening, Baron. How do! how do!"

The old Baron stopped drumming on the table, and glared at the calm intruder with a glare that would have frozen the blood of any ordinary man; but Mr. Palladium received the scowl with the imperturbability that distinguished him. The menials trembled still more to think that any man would be foolhardy enough to encroach on the Baron's privacy at such a moment. The old Baron's menials spent most of their spare time in trembling when the Baron was at home. "Well, sir," thundered the Baron, bringing down his clenched fist on the table, "what means this intrusion?" _ _ _

"You see, Baron," answered L. W., "I come from America. Now America is a great country. We all admit it. A Chicago man is noted for his bashfulness, but even lie will admit that America is a great country. Still there is one thing we lack in America. We are short of castles. You might not believe it, but there is not in all Chicago such a fine old castle as this." " You surprise me," said the Baron, with a sinister smile. "The old gent's thawing out," remarked Mr. Palladium to himself. Then he continued aloud, "It's so, we haven't. Castles are not our specialty out there. Of course we have some very fine private residences, but nothing old—nothing venerable—no moss-grown ruins —no ivy-mantled towers—no splendour falls on castle walls business, nor no snowy summits, old in story. Why, Baran, the most ancient house in Chicago isn't thirty years old." "Really, really," gasped the Baron, thunderstruck, not so much with the information, as the easy familiarity of the Chicago man. "True as you live," Baron continued Palladium, who, without being invited„ seated himself in one of the baronial chairs, and put up his feet on another. "Well, sir, I thought if I ever came to Europe, I would call on some of the effete, nobility over here, and ask for an invitation to stay all night at a regular old castle. X'm willing to pay first-class hotel prices, and take the haunted chamber. Do you happen to have one on the premises, Baron ?" "Several," said the Baron. "An assortment, eh? Gosh! you're well fixed. Well, I suppose we can strike up a bargain for a night's lodgings, eh, Baron? They tell me most of you fellows are as poor as crows, anyhow—living on pride and sauerkraut, principally, so I suppose the money won't come amiss. "It will be very welcome," replied the Baron, with ominous grimness. "Caitiff, the keys." The Caitiff approached, trembling, of course, and, kneeling on one knee, handed the Baron a great bunch of keys. "Follow me," said the Baron sternly; and Palladium followed him down a long passage, and then along another' and through several rooms, and at last they stopped before a narrow oaken door, into which the Baron began fitting the keys. "You are not going to come any dungeon cell business on me," said the Chicago man, who was beginning to be a little uneasy over the demeanour of the Baron. "I don't care about staying in a dungeon, as I understand they are apt to be a little damp, and, you see, I have .a touch of rheumatism." "The room I shall give rou replied the Baron, "will be dry and airy." When the narrow door was opened it showed a stone stairway that led lip into the darkness. The stairway Ir-d wound round and round and up and up, until the Chicago man thought he had never felt so tired in his life. Still the old Baron toiled on a few steps above him, and although he could not see him, he could hear, the jingle of the keys. Every now and then they came to a little slit in the heavy stone wall of the tower, and through these chinks Mr. Palladium got glimpses of the Rhine valley, and saw that they were already up a great height. "Hold on, Baron," cried the Chicago man at last. "Fm about tuckered out: Let's rest a bit. George Washington! but this is a steep climb. Now, if I were von, Baron, I would put an elevator in this tower." "A what ? ' said the Baron. • "An elevator. A lift. An ancencior, or whatever they call it in France. You could run one very cheaply here. L That stream that comes down the hill would fix you all . right. Hydraulic elevator, you know." "Are you ready?" asked the Baron. ' "Well, I will try another whack at it. Is it much ) further up? .1 believe this tower is higher than the one on the Board Of Trade in Chicago. They have an ) elevator there, though." At last they'reached the top. The Baron put another key in another look, and the rusty bolt grated harshly ,back

"That's business," said Mr. P. "There's some romance about a rusty old lock. Oil would make it easier, but it would spoil the thrilling novelistio flavour of the thing." With some effort the old Baron pushed up a trap-door, and the evening light that came in showed step that led to the opening. He motioned to his guest tc attend. Mr. Palladium found himself at the top of a rotz . tower at a great height above the rest of the castle. There was a splendid view on all sides, and down immediately below him were the numerous roofs of the castle and their stacks of chimneys, from some of which smoke was lazi* ascending. The winding Rhine, silvery in the evening glow, showed here and there the twinkling lights that each moment were becoming more numerous as the shades of night crept on. "Fine view you have here, Baron," said Mr. P. There was no answer, and, turning round, he sem that the Baron had not followed him. More than that, the:trap.. door was closed, and the next instant he heard the rusty bolt thrust back into its place. "See here, Baron," cried the man from Chicago, "no tricks, you know. You are not going to leave me here all night. I hope !" A mocking laugh was the only reply. "You oat leave me up here, you know!" shouted the now thoroughly frightened Palladium. But Mr. P. was wrong. The Baron not only could, but he did. The man from America heard his slowly retreating footsteps echo more and more faintly es the Baron went down the winding stone stairway of that fatal tower. [To be concluded sere waled

Mrs. Folsom, wife of Mr. John Folsom, Gray's Inn Passage, Bedford Row, London, suffered front the effects ot a sprained ankle for nineteen years. Many I different remedies were tried without success. On applying St. Jacobs Oil, pain vanished, the swelling was rearmed, and her ankle is as strong as ever. For sale everywhere. If you have nothing worth saying, say it, i.e., nothing. Science may analyse the blood within our veins, but the thoughts of our heait do baffle her research. "Now, how must I do with this wedding cake to dream on it ?" asked a gushing damsel of a matter-of- fact young man. "Just eat It; that's all," was the reply. lMinister: "And do you like to go to church with your papa and manima, Bobby ?" Bobby (inclined to be non-committal) : I guess I like it as well as pa 'does." ' Many of the evils in society, much of the vice and crime which we deplore, come from the degrading niture of the amusements entered into. To inveigh against ' them avails little; but to substitute something better, and to persuade men to choose it, is a task worthy of all endeavour. For all kinds of domestic sewing, Bagleysnd Wright $ cotton • the best.—Adst.

Things' went: en in this way for nine or tea menths,, and then a dreadful thing happened. The Frenchman went to bed one night as well as he possibly could.be, it seemed, and the next morning he waif clOad. It was a shocking blow, and Eustace was almost wild with 'grief. - The dootor who came to see the. dead man ,saul that he died of heart disettae, and that was the verdict at the inquest. The Frenchman left, a letter for father behind him, in which he said he Would 'die of heart disease, and that he would die suddenly ; and he left Eustace in father's' care, and solemnly implored him to take care of Eustace, and not to desert him. Father, when he read , the letter, took , Eustace's hand and Said that Eustace *lonia reniain With him as long as he wished, and :was- surprised that Eustace should .burst put crying; "Do you not wish to remain with me?" 'father asked.. "Yes, for over, for ever I" Eustace said. Well; everything went on nicely for another three months, and then one evening when father ,same home from work he found Eustace lying in a fever. Eustace was delirious' and father began to undress him to get him into bed, but he soon left off, and in great trouble he ran into the township and got a doctor. Would you believe it, Eustace wasn't a boy at all, he was a young lady ! so I must now speak of her in that may ; but she was always Eustace with father after that. She was very, very ill, and father nursed her ; he could not get a woman to do it, there were so few of them on the gold-diggings; and when she , got :well-which was not :far a good many Weekstather married her, and he is n2y mother.-Whila. . _ The two little ones had edged up to her by this time, and were staring worse than ever at the visitor. Lizbeth put a protecting arm about thim, as a mother might have done, her own little legs dangling below her the while, " Make a curchey to the ladies, Vicky," she said to the baby. "Site do curchey beautiful when she likes" (to us), "but her bein' so young, I 'ates'to mike her like. That linagy there's in two syllables, he is, but he's that shy he'll never do it for strangers. Curchey, Vicky dear, wont you? Oh, fie! to be so silly I" The baby was giving symptoms of being about to burst into tears, and Lizbeth took her in her arms and carried her all about the room until she had recovered from Nina's incautious advances toward better acquaint- ance. This done, she was put down on the floor with an empty can and slew peas to amuse herself, and Lizbeth went • back to her work, with a parting embrace and kiss. "Isn't she dreadfully heavy for you to carry ? " asked Nina, noticing how she had swayed over on one side under her burden. "'Er 'eavy ? Oh no, miss! not a bit. I've 'ad 'em 'eau, Tummas was like lead, he was. And Hang), the same, till he fell away to nothink at all. But 'er ; slfe's not. It 'ud be all I'd ask if I 'ad the time," she replied. And then, with a sudden impulse and a flush of motherly pride, she dropped her sewing, and running over, picked Vicky up and brought het to us, saying, " Whatever was I a-thinkin' of not to show you 'or teeth, miss! Look at 'em I ,A'int she getting beautiful? And never a fit! I've 'ad 'ern with fits dreadful. Hangy 'ad 'em awful both with his uppers and lowers,and betwigxt and between till I was frightened to 'ave him out o' my sight, was." She was replacing the lumpy, shapeless, very ugly, aid wholly unattractive baby, who was evidently. a model infant in her eyes, when, with one of her quick movements, she caught sight of Angy tiptoeing before the open cupboard near the fire- place; she exclaimed, "Drat the child I " and darting across the room,- she pounced upon him, shook him briskly, cried: "Always in the cupboard or the fire I 'fake that, sir "(a box), " and turn rour face to the wall till you are let to come out." It was comical to see the little thing's severe air, and the way in which she marched the culprit into a corner like a small domestic gendarme,though he was a well-grown boy, who might very well have turned the tables if the idea of revolting against Liz- beth's authority had ever entered his mind. That young person, however, was endowed with such an indomitable spirit, and such force of character, that I have not the least doubt she appeared quite twelve feet high to the other children, and was as imposing as the rector,or the 'parish beadle,or what they called "the perliee." Having given him a farewell thump on the bead with her thimble, she came back to us, and noticing our smiles, said gravely: "Oh, that Rangy 'are got to be kept down, miss; not but what he's a good boy, only wautin' to 'aye his own way, ml 'owever 'e's to he kep' from burnin' up alive is what I don't see, nor can't say."—Harper's Magazine, Christmas Number.

div.head: SAVED FROM SUICIDE.
div.p: SAVED FROM SUICIDE.

"Lily," vaid Katie, stopping, " They are having service it tile church by the Abbey. Listen. Oh, it must be the evening service. They are praising God and singing hymns, and we are out in the fog and the' cold, and going to kill ourselves. "Yes, I could not sing any hymns just now." "Lily, let us have one prayer *before we go." "No; leap first and pray afterwards ; there will be plenty of time to pray when we are sure that we shall not have to come back to this miserable world any more." She dragged the bther girl along with her past the Abbey straight down to the Embankment. "Hush, Katie; don't speak now. This is the very place." She stopped at one of the landing places, where the steps go down into the water. "The tide is running," said Lily. (How did she know, because they could see nothing "It will carry us up the river ;it will roll us over and over. Don't let go my hand, Katie ; it will kill us in P moment, and then it will drive us and beat us and bang us against the piers of Westminster Bridge, so that no one will be able to recognise us when they do find us. And so it will never be known what became of us. Dear Katie—dear Katherine Regina—poor queen without a penny—give me one kiss. Hold my hand. Now you shall be with your lover in a moment and all your sorrow shall he over. Hold my hand and run down the steps with me. Quick ! Quick ! Hold my baud hard—harder. Quick I' She drew Katie to the steps, crying .out to her to hasten and to hold fast, and dragging her down to the river; Katie was too weak to resist mentally and bodily. And all around her lay the thick black fog like a wall of darkness. " Did you elir think what it would be to he shut up in such an Intern° as Dante's in a thick black fog, a darkness wrapping you round as with a horrible cloak from which there was no escape. All day long these girls had been sitting in such a fog, withoat food, and before them they heard and now saw with eyes of madness the rush of the river, which would mercifully take them out of the fog and land them at the foot of the Golden gates ? " Quick, Katie, quick, don't let go. On ! " The fog lifted a little, suddenly, at this moment. Before the girls stood a figure, black and gaunt, which stretched out two long arms, and said with harsh and strident voice, " No, my dears, not this time you don't." Then Lily loosed her hold of Katie's hand, and thraw .out her arms in a gesture of hopelessness. "Oh !" she cried, " God will not let us live and He will not let us die." Then she turned and fled, leaving Katie alone.—" Katherins Regina." By W. Besant. Arrowsmith's Christmas itn

• CHAPTER XVI.„ ntz:kr TO EARTH. ( Two days later' Anne Derrick left Row-Tor Farm at an early hour. She drove to St, Stephen's railwa.y. station with Richards in the "trap," and started on • her journey ,to Bath. She had kept her last discovery a ,seeret from every one, and she said' merelY that she was hoping to gain some information respecting Susan from her former mistress. ft was about half-past three in the afternoon when she arrived at Bath. Carrying her little black travel: ling bag in her hand, she found. her way to a post- office, where She aiiked to see a *Beth directory. With fingers trembling with excitement, she turned over its pages. Yes, here was the name of Mrs. Norton, and at the same address-24, Lansdown-crescent. Anne set off at once for a walk as steep and toil. , Some, although houses lined 'the Way; as•aSeeridinorf one of the Dartmoor tors. On she went, upapd. up, until she had reached the stately semi-circle of mansions, which -had a sloping green lawn and- ancient elm. trees just , below them' and beyond a wide expanse of wOoded hills stretching far away westward, with the city. spread out in a misty hollow some hundreds of feet beneath the Crescent. It had been a calm and ..bright December, day.; the sun, /declining towards the opposite hill, shed a ruddy lustre on the quaint, last century buildings', many of them leafy with climbing jessamine, magnolia,and, pomegranate. Anne went along the broad pavement looking for No. 24. ;t was no slivht ordeal to the country•bred woman to ring at:the bell, and tciask the sn4ef: cilious- looking footman who opened the door; it Miis: Norton would see her. Going down the riverside in the darkness at Tavistock, to keep an appointmer.t With an unknown; was nothing :Compared .te• this. But Anne's whole mind and soul were s) entirelylabsorbed in the work she had to accomplish, the regaining of Martin's freedom, that sho would have'been ready to go to Windsor Castle, and request to see the Queen, if that would have served her 'purpose. Anne was sliewn into a large and prettily furnis,hed drawing-room, Where in a hot.house atrit6sphdre,. and ' amidst hot-house flowers, sat a handsome, though rather hard-featured woman of sixty, in a black vel- vet gown, with iron-grey hair beneath a delicate lace cap. The name "Miss Derrick," by which Anne was announced, conveyed no idea to her. mind, and she looked surprised and somewhat haughty ~when her visitor entered. Anne was as refined and as calm in manner as any princess, and she was dressed' in what Mrs. Lawson called "very handsome mourning," still she spoke with a West-coMitry accent, and, of course, . was not, technically speaking, a gentle-- wom an. madam," she began, " if

I have come to ask you, m. , _ you could kindly tell me something about ,aly sister Susan, who lived with you as maid in the year 1876." Mrs. Norton startedaind drew herself up. "Really," she replied, in a freezing tone, "I cannot be expected to remember the various servants 1 have had in toy life." ' "The matter is very impertant or I would not have ventured to trouble you. My sister has lately. flied. Since her death I have found Get that she married whilst she was in your service. Did you know it, may I ask, madam?" "I? Certainly not. All I know about Susan Derrick is that she grossly misconducted herself .and that I sent her away at a day's notice. I remember so much, if that is any satisfaction to you." Anne's face flushed a little, but she went ' on very calmly. "The fact of my sister's' marriage in that year is beyond a doubt. Did: you ever now anything of a gentleman named Francis Carteret? Because he is the man Susan Married.. Mrs. Nerton started to her feet, her face became crimson. ." How dare you,", she cried. "How dare you. name Captain Carteret in the same breath with that woman? Captain Carteret marry a ser- vant ! I have never been so insulted in my life !" She turned to the fireplace, and palled the bell so violently, that the footman appeared without a moment's loss-of time. "Show that person out imme- diately, said Mrs. Norton. Anne replied only, "-I have the marriage certificate in my pocket, Mra Norton," and then she departed with unfutHed tdigiity, thinking too munch of the information she had gained to be much troubled. the insult to herself. She had advanced, a .further step, , although, as before, she bad been baffled in the very moment of succe.ss. Mrs. Norton was a friend of the man who had married Susan, that much was certain. • Else, why her anger? And wily did she call him Captain Carteret, when Anne had mentioned him oiily by his Christian name ? • ' There was now nothing for Anne to do, but (to use an ancient term of warfare) to "sit down before" the stronghold she hoped to take. "I may have to remain in Bath a week or two," thought she, rather sadly, " when I had hoped to go to Exeter to-morrow to aee Martin, and tell him all I had found out. I may have .to act a part, and that is the worst thing I have had to do yet. But if I did not do it myself, I should have to lit a detec- tive to do it for me ; and he wouldn't have the excuse that I should have—that it was done to save the one that's nearest and dearest to me in the whole world. No, whatever lies have to be told for Martin's sake, I'll tell them myself and settle the matter with-my own conscience afterwards." There was a pastryeook's shop, of a homely and un- pretentious sort, which Anne passed as she was de- scending the steep road which led from Lansdown Crescent to the city qf Bath. She was reminded by. it that she had not touched food since her early breakfast at Row-Tor Farm; and a cup of tea and a roll would be very welcome. And, while she drank the tea, she made a few trivial remarks to !Mrs. Brown, the mistress of the shop; but these .re- ' marks were the beginning of Anne's campaign. "I am quite a stranger in Bath,", she said. "This is the first time I have ever been here." "You are from Devonshire, surely," answered Mrs. Brown. "I knew it by your way of speaking. Do you happen to know Okehatupton ?". "Yes, very well ; " and then Anne felt thankful that it was not Tavistock that she Was to be ques- tioned about. "To think I 'should have met some 1 one who knows the dear old place! I was born and bred at a farm a few miles away, right under Cawsand Beacon. Well, well, I shall never see it • again. I suppose, all my friends there are dead or gone away; but it does my heart good to meet some one from the old country. I shall never forget how sweet the air , smelt on the moor—we never seem to get a breath of real fresh air in Bath—and the heather all in a blaze of purple, and the whortlebenies, and the yellow clotted cream we had for tea." There was a little more talk of this sort, and then Mrs. Brown inquired, "And what's brought you to Bath ? " "I want to get a situation as lady s-mball, replied Anne without hesitation, though her cheeks burned as she uttered the first untruth she had spoken in her life. "I have'excellent references to shew you," and she took from her pocket the letter of recom- mendation written by Miss Evelyn, Susan's late mis- tress, which Anne had found, and had, brought with her, thinking it might possibly prove a useful weapon. "Can you tell me of a quiet lodging, where I could stay whilst I was looking out for a situation?" Mrs. Brown was so favourably impressed by Anne's appearance, and by the feet of her being a Devonshire woman' that she said at once that she had a little bedroom at the top of the house to let, which Miss Derrick could havd; if she pleased. "Nothing could suit me better," replied Anne, with secret satisfaction. "Do you think I have any chance of getting a good situation in Bath ? I dare say, now, you know all about numbers of the families in this neighbourhood." "Well, yes, we serve a tidy few of them with bread. I am thinking now—there is a young lady Just come to live in one of the houses up there in the Crescent, she and her pa have just taken it furnished for the winter—very rich folks, I under- stand, name of Hartley. \Nre have got most of their custom, luckily, for I happened to know their cook before she went to live with them; and I did hear that the young lady was going to be mar- red soon after the New year. Now, I Wonder whether she'd be likely to want a maid? But I shouldn't be surprised if the cook dropped in for half-an-houithrs, evening. She told me she'd be at leisure, as the family was dining out to-night, and then I'll ask her , what she thinks about it," Mrs. Brown shewed, Anne upstairs .to a small but very clean and neatly furnished little attic. A lire was lighted, and then „ Anne, feeling very weary and exhausted, laid down upon the bed and slept for Ready two hours.

"My 'husband is out this evening," said thte pastrycook's wife, "so I am particular glad of your - company," and then again she fell talking of Oka- hamyton, until she was interrupted by somebody' coming into the shop. ... Jr another minute Mrs. Brown returned to thew parlour; bringing with her a 'very important-100ki,4 • * pezsonage in ,a black., silk gown' hisley slier and bonnet laden with flowers, whom "the baker I wife iiitiddiicecrto-Arine as the Cook from Mr: Hart— ley's in Lanadown-crescent. This young' person is wanting a situation a' lady's Maid," said Mrs. Brown. Well, she isn't what You'd call a very intimate friend; I( Can't say as 'she is-only she knows my old home near Okehampton as well as you know Bath,Aintl I feel quite tut interest in her.", Anne sat in. a dark corner of the Parlines her cheek S burning, feeling acutely the false positii3n ill which she was placed. Here Anne rose • froM her corner •, as she can for- ward infii the light, Mrs. Brown observed that her face was deadly pale, and there was a strange`gleame in her es es • "Why, how ' bad you do look, to be sure ! yOu ain't going •to 'faint, are you?" Mrs. Brown's kind heart was filled with concern. 'But Anne answered in a tolerably firm voice, " think I will go out for, a little turn in the air. shall feel all right directly, thank you." ".Dear me, I'd go out with you and welcome, only Brown's away, and I can't leave the shop." Anne thanked her again, and then escaped from -the: room She flew, upstairs, put on her bonnet and cloak as quickly as her trembling hands would allow her ; then 'she ran downstairs again, out int° the lanip-lit street, and so down the hill to the post' office,. which she had passed on her way from the raiiwKy station to Lansdown-crescent. Her work was done so' far; she had run the preY to earth; the 'task of actually capturing hit'n must be. handed over to another. Arrived at the, post-office she took a telegraph form from the counter, and without stopping !‘" ' reckon up the number of her words—canna °nil to make her ,message clear, and, above all, urgeeu —she wrote the following telegram, thiaing as she addressed it, " He shall have this to-night at his owe lionSe, not n moment shall be lost" • . THE STATE OF EITROPE.—SECRET MASS- ING OF TROOPS.—HOLIDAY QUIETNESS. —TURKEYS POSITION. Cowsra.artwortx, SUNDAT. Turkey has become seriously alarmed at the -war preparations of her neigh- bours. By order of his Majesty, the question of CaHim! out 50,000 men is now being considered. These would he sent partly to Erzeromn, and partly to Bulgaria. Th, Russian movements of troops in Asia Minor and Bessa- rabia are taken with the fact that Russia continues to urge the Porte to act against the existing order of -things in Bulgaria, and is Making a new demand for the payment of the arrears of the war indemnity. M. de Nelidoff has informed the Porte that if these arrears of £750.000 are not paid Russia will be obliged ultimately to take pledges in Asia Minor for the protection of her interest. Si. PETRUSIMSO, SUNDAY,—A well-known Turkish statesman, speaking here upon the political situation, and the position which Turkey would most likely assume in case of a European war, declared that she certainly wrould not remain neutral. If she did so it would un- doubtedly cost her dear. The Porte thinks that the chances would be almost equal in a war between Russia and France on the one side and the Central Powers on the other. Thus the Turkish alliance must prove highly.. desirable to both parties. Turkey is accordingly firmly resolved to secure her own interests in the manner she may think most advantageous. ST PETRRSTIIIRG, MONDAT.—Tt may possibly assist in ctahaing the excitement which seems to prevail in cer- tain capitals •if what one of the most latrintis Russian generals has just said is repeated with reference to the present state of Europe. "It is pry full conviction." he declared, " that neither Austria nor Germany intends 1,- :stake war. The Czarhimself is more pacifically disposed than ever, and it would be simply criminal of Russian -Statesmen to try and induce hint to commence war." • LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL TN RUSSIA. .---RECEPTION BY THE CZAR.' ST. PETNUSINTRG, FRIDAY.--I.ord, it. • Churchill arrived here by this evening's frontier train, and drove to his .appartments in the lintel de France. The Russians have been greatly exercised during the last few days ,as to the object of his Lordship's visit, and despite all denials continue to snspect metives. To-day's Graskla nine contains a reminder of Lord Randolph's -public speeches against Russia, and cautions its reVers, while dispensing the traditional Russian hospitality to their distinguished visitor, not to forget his recent Parliamentary attitude. ST. PaTvasinilirl. SATCRIIAT.—The Notate Vretna, to- -day, Commenting upon Lord Randolph Churchill's visit to St. Petersburg. states that it is by no means firmly con- -winced that his lordship has come on a diplomatic-mission. The journal adds, however, that, should there be such a mission, it can, in its opinion, only be advantageous for Russia entirely to reassure England as to the absolute safety of her Jmlian posse zsions, provided that the British Cabinet, give sitfficient guarantee that in future it will ,not onpose Russia in international questions which •directly concern her. ST. Parrrisanuo, SCNDAT.—Lord Randolph Churchill yesterday had-an interview with M. de Giers. His lord- ship and Lady Churchill milt probably be received by ;the Czar to-morrow at Gat chino. ST. PF.TEUSIRTRG. MONDAY !;MIT.--Lord and Lady Randolph Churchill went to Gatschina to-day at noon by special direct invitation of the Czar. Their -appearance here almost engrosses the attention of aociety and the nress, and in fact constitutes quite a godsend tor the 'latter at a moment when the Christmas ,holidays abroad have temporarily stopped the supply of ,Wegeaphic news and alarms from the other capitals. , Reporters and telegram agents hover potind his lordship .411 dti, but the Gradettrals..says they are not admitted.

A well-known Moscow editor has arrived here to-dtp .11Pecially to have an interview with the distinguished aV:ion the Central Asian question. Hi g lorcLship has y visited M. de filers and received a return call from the Foreign Minister. VrertteA, MONPAX INPIRT.—The audience which Lord arld Lath- Randolph Churchill had to-day at Gntschina pins in Importance. It is probably true that Lord R. Churchill had no political mission in Russia, &titan Eng- lish statesman of his peat and probable future cannot meet the Czar without gaining impressions on the ques- tion of the day. which might serve to enlighten not only his own Government, but others on friendly terms with England. It matters little-whether it be General Von Echweinits or Lord R. Churchill tirronf,th whom Germany and Austria learn what the Czar Vants and what his in- tentions are. The purpide would be perfectly served if the Czar would condeseend to open his Mind to an Eng- lish statesman as to one less interested and more im- partial in the conflict of interests between Russia and Austria than either General Van Schweinitz or Count /On Wolkenstein. Should, however, the Czar's reserve be, maintained towards General Von Schweinitz the in- •Ovitable conclusion will be that the desitms of Russia are dangerous to European peace, and in this case Austria would not wait until it pleases her antagonist to show her cards. The Czar will have to say within the next week or two what he wants, and what the moving of troops on the frontier means, or we shall have war in March at the latest.

AMERICA AND CANADA.--GREAT RAIL- : . WAY STRIKE—THE LOST RAFT. NEW YORK. StiliDAL—The greatest strike in the his- tory of Pennsylvania, except that of 1877, began on . Saturday, when the Knights of Labour who control the men on the Reading Railway ordered all hands Ito stop work, save those in the passenger and mail service of the line. The strike affects about 85,000 'men. including many coat miners. The cause of the • 'strike •is similar to that on Mr. Gould's Missouri 'Pacifie lines some years ago. It began in an attempt of the Knights of r.alhour to boycott a firm of grain elevators on the '141,6 who employed non-unionist men. '/n order tn bring the firm to terms five gangs of men of The Reading Company refused to move the waggons jowled with dour belongim, to the firm. The superin- tendent discharged the men, whereupon 65,000 men were Ordered by the Knights of Labour to quit until the re- instatement of the discharged men was granted. Saw 'Volts, Mompar.—Roth sides seem confident of winning, but the chances are heavily against the strikers. The company has valuable assistance. The Labour Organisation is bitterly opposed to the Knights of Labour, and is supping men to take the places of the - strikers. The company say they have enough new men to begin operations on the line on Tuesday, and there are grave fears of disturbances if they do, AA the strikers are desperate, believing, if they lose this tight, the 'Knights of Labour will be destroyed as an organisation, they having been rapidly disintegrating during the past year. • • Nr.v YON, SENDAY.—Captain Mathews, of the British Schooner Mistletoe, which arrived at Boston on Friday from Rio Grande, reports that on Sunday last, in lai. s 39-55 east, long. 68'30, F•lie passed four large pieces of timber, about 50ft. ion.. • -•*).n MIL GLADSTONE'S HOLIDAY. JOURNEY FROM HAWARDFS. Mr. Gladstone left Hawarden Castle, on Monday morn- ing, on his way to the Continent, the first stage of the journey being performed in aclosed carriage. Accom- panied by Mrs Gladstone, Miss Gladstone, and Mr. W. 1. GlAstorie, he drove shortly after ten o'clock to Broughton Hall Station, on the London and North- Western Railway. Here a special 'saloon carriage was provided, and a quick run was made to Chester, where a great crowd assembled. The city was visited by many holiday people from surrounding towns. As soon as I air. Gladstone was recognised his admirers broke forth into cheering, and at the central platform a rush was made for the window. Mr. Gladstone appeared at the window, and begged those around him to keep away from the carriage in order that the traffic might be carried on in the usual way. After a few minutes matters quietened down, and, re- sponding to numerous invitations, Mr. Gladstone ap- peared at the window and said: Well, ladies and gentlemen: you .have come here in great force, and I think it an act of remarkable kindness on your part, Ishich I shall not readily forget. (Cheers.) I hope that. When a great occasion comes, viz., when Chester has an opportunity Of giving her voice for a member of Pasha': ment, you will come here in greater force still. You have a great part of a great work to do. (Cheers.)—At this Moment the train moved on. Mr. Gladstone was in good voice and able to make himself distinctly heard by ,the throng. Crewe was reached at noon, the start from Chester riaving been made at 1130, and here there was a re- Dewed manifestation of enthusiasm. Immediately the train pulled up the saloon was besieged, and people clambered up to the door. Mr. Gladstone, in response to repeated cheers, let the window down, whereupon a gen- tleman cried out, "Three cheers; compliments of tie. season; a sure journey and a safe return; and in antici- pation of the 29th (referring, of course, to Mr. Glad- stone's birthday, 'Many happy returns of the day.'" Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply, said: It is very kind of you, gentlemen, to use this passing moment for the purpose of giving me a Chirstmas greeting. I accept it with the utmost pleasure, and allow me to offer you my good wishes in return. (Cheers.) We cannot help mixing even now in our private and personal affairs our anxiety with regard to public affairs, and if you will allow me I will gay one thing which ought to he in the mouth of everyone who is a voter—and now nearly everyone is a voter for the benefit of the country if he likes. Whether a man agrees with the present system of governing Ireland is an affair for his own conscience and responsibility. But if he does not, then it is his business to exert himself to put an end to it. At Rugby there was almost an entire absence of demonstration. Only a few people were on the plat- form. At Euston terminus there was a great crowd, and the arrival platform was kept as clear as possible by the railway officials, assisted by a sm ill forle of the metropolitan police. However, when the train steamed in, a number of people had managed to make their was- past the authorities. 'Just a few minutes previous to the arrival of the train Mr. Arnold Morley, M.P.. the chief Liberal Whip, drove up to receive Mr. Gladstone and upon the train stopping •he at once entered tie saloon. The ex-Premier on leaving the saloon was loudly cheered, and during a few minutes of waiting before entering the carriage which was in readiness to convey him to Charing Cross, he was the recipient of mingle,' cheers and groans. At Charing Cross precautions were adopted by the authorities to prevent any inconvenience to the travel's lees. A special train was hi waiting. Mr. Gladstone. accompanied by Mr. Arnold Morley, arrived at lee minutes to four, and his appearance was greeted with cheering, which, however, was met with groaning and hooting. Shortly afterwards Mr. Chillers came up an,i entered into conversation with the ex-Premier. Amens others who were on the platform were Lord Oxenbridge and Mr. Hugh Watt, M.P., and in a few minutes thel were joined by Earl and Countess Spencer. Mr. Glad- stone warmly shook hands with Lord Spencer. who re- mained in the saloon in conversation with his leadee until the train left. Mrs. Gladstone, accompanied by Miss Gladstone and Mr. W. H. Gladstone, drove up in a second carriage shortly after four o'clock. and then sem( refreshment in the shape of tea was served in the saloon. The crowd outside meanwhile indulged in CTICPN and groans. Precisely at a quarter-past four Mr. Gladstone bade adieu to. his friends, and the train moved sway, th, destination being the seat of Lord Northbourne, Betteshanger, Bandwieh:

SPEECH AT DOVER. s Mr. Gladstone proceeded from Betteshahger Park to Dover by special train on Tuesday for the purpose of re- ceiving an address from the Kent Liberals. There was a hostile demonstration outside Dover Station, during which Mr. Gladstone was struek on the • shoulder by a snowball. In the course of his speech at the Town Hall, the right hon, gentleman said there was daily proofs of individual cases in which intelligent Comei•vatives, re- flecting upon their position, found that an idle and mis- chievous superstition prevented them doing justice to Ireland. Dealing with Lord Salisbury's recent speech at Oxford, Mr. Gladstone held that the absence of cavil and criticism on the part of the Liberals in reference to the foreign policy of the Government showed that they did not, debase the interests of the country to those of party. He did not counsel a policy of indifference with regard to matters which involved largely the interests, of the human race, but he hoped that England would not be drawn into a continental quarrel except upon the clearest dictates of British duty, interest, and honour. He complained of Lord Salisbury's ambiguity on the subject of Fair Trade, and declared that as ,it was im- possible to rely on the existing Government for the con- tinued existence of Free Trade, the masses must decide whether Protection should be revived and sent forth as a prescription for curing the economical health of the country. He denied, that the Liberal party gave any countenance to obstruction, and, proceeding to deal at some length with Irish affairs, said that Lord Salisbuty speech cleared the issue, and showed that it was intended to make coercion permanent. The aim of the Coercion Act was narrowing and taking away the civil rights of the Irish people. Lord Salisbury held that this empire must be consolidated as France was consoli- dated; but Francehadnotbeen consolidatedby joining to- gether broken pieces thatfrom centurytocentury resisted consolidation and strove to preserve a national history of their own. Then as to the case of Italy; that country was consolidated because it liad been violently broken to pieces, and each part of Italy had for its aspiration the reunion of the country. Lord Salisbury forgot that Russia; from whom a lesson might be taken in such a , matter, was toowise to consolidate Finland ; that Sweden ' and Norway were all consolidated: that Austria, and Hungary had almost the freedom of independent powers; that Belgium and Holland might have remained united if Holland had had the wisdom to grant to Belgium her local institutions: that even Turkey had found in giving willingly autonomy to her provinces the secret of giving them contentment. That was what Ireland was asking I for. Lord Salisbury was candid enough to go on to in- timate that the present state of things ntust continue whether Ireland liked it or not •, he did not condescend to set forth the ridiculous Action that there there were two million anti-Home Rulers in Ireland. -He (Mr. Gladstone) did not believe there were 500,000 real anti-Home Rulers in Ireland. At least half of the Protestant populace were ready to embrace Home Rule if it had the seal of the legislature, and those who remained were the old, obstinate, uncured, but he trusted not incurable Orangemen, who had been for thre generations the greatest mischiefs. (Cheers.) Under the most cruel pressure of tyranny and torture in every form' without being invested with the suffrage or Power, the Irish people had maintained its identity and ' the integrity of its traditions. The representative sys- tem of Ireland now for the first time gave full effect to , the convictions and desires of the people. Ireland *clew her own strength, and the tremendous evils from which she was suffering were only mitigated by the firm know- ledge of the people that there was on this side of the Channel a large and determined party friendly to law, and order on one side and to national rights on the other. But when the Irish people saw the Lord Mayor of Dub- lin sent to prison, was not this calculated to widen the breach that separated them from the law of the country? The whole of the power and voice of the people of Ireland was on one side; on the other side was the voice of Lord Salis- bury, which came to them with a foreign sound. (Cheers.) In conclusion, Mr. Gladstone said he repre- sented that this voice of Lord Salisbury VMS in conflict with all the living facts ' it was in conflict with what they , saw happening upon e.;.,e,h opportunity as it came for I the expression of the popular voice; it was in conflict with the fixed determination of the Liberal party, which had never yet inscribed upon its banners the name of a cause without carrying its banners to victory. (Cheers.) Sustained alike by facts and principles, by convictions and traditions, Irishmen, though forbidden by Lord Salisbury, would hope.. must hope, ought to hope, and in the train of that hope would come to victory, and in the train of victory liberty, and in the tram of liberty I peace. and in the train of peace the restitution of that good name to England, which would then indeed be re- lieved from the last blot resting upon it, because there would then no longer remain a disgraceful exception to the effects of her political genius, and to the steadiness of that love of liberty which was founded upon princi- ples of freedom as well as justice throughout her wide and universal empire. (Loud and prolonged cheers.) The proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to Mr. Gladstone, on the motion of Lord Granville, after which the right hon. gentleman returned to I34ttes- hanger.

Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs. and Miss Glad- stone, left Sandwich by special train at 10-25 on Wednes- day morning for Folkstone, on his way to Italy, At various points on the journey the right hon. gentleman was heartily cheered. He reached Boulogne a little be- fore two o'clock in the afternoon, and lost no time in continuing his journey south. Considerable indignation is expressed throughout East Kent amongst all classes of politicians at the unmannerly behaviour of the handful of roughs who pelted Mr. Gladstone with snowballs at Dover on Tuesday. Dover Liberals maintain that the opposition was deliberately organised and paid for by the local Conservatives.

• k THE LIBERAL PARTY : GAINS IN 1887. Dnring the year now drawing to a close the strength at the Liberal party in Parliament has increased by no fewer than ten votes, counting 20 on a division. In Janbary last the Ministerial majority was 118; it is now 98. This significant change has been brought about by a liTheral lam of four seats at by-elections and by the secessipn of six Dissentient Liberals; and it is all the mote remarkable from the fact that the Conservative party have gained no additional seat at any contest since the, General Eleetion. Indeed, one Conservative 'nem- her,' Mr. Evelyn, is resigning his seat for Deptford from inability to support the Government any longer in their Irilh policy. On the other hand, one of the Liberal intimbers for Dundee, Mr. Lacaita, is also about, to resign his seat; but Mr. Lacaita does not take this step because of :any approval of the coercive policy of the Govern- mint. The strength of the four parties in Parliament at the close as compared with the beginning of the year may be gathered from the following table, which shows the position of each political group in Janusry and De- cember:—
January. Dezember. Liberal. . . ........... l9O 200 Nationalista Dissentient Liberals.— ... __

Conservatives 316-394 314—.384 Fimr seats are vacant, or about to be vacated, and. for the purpose of comparison, theyare included in the above , table, thns—Winchester, vacant by the death of Colonel ' Tottenham, and Deptford, held till the meeting of Par- liament by Mr. Evelyn, are ranked as Conservative: Dundee and West Edinburgh, Mr. Buchanan being now 't supporter of Mt. Gladstone's policy, are ranked as Liberal. It may be noted here that at the last election the Liberal majority at Dundee was 4,671. and that last year Mr. Buchana.n's majority in West Edinburgh was 690, and in the previous year 1,175. Reverting to the above table, it will be noticed that the Dissentient Liberal vote has decreased by eight. Two seats for- merly held by Dissentient Liberals—Burnley, by the late Mr..Rylands, and the Northwich Division of Cheshire, by the late Mr. Verdin—have been won by Liberals, Mr. Slagg and Mr. Brunner respectively. Six members who Were returned as Dissentient Liberals—Mr. Winter- hot ham, Mr. C. R. Talbot, Sir Hussey Vivian, Mr. Hing- ley, Mr. Buchanan, and Sir Thomas Grove—may now be classed as Liberals, and thus the decrease of eight in the Dissentient Liberal vote is accounted for. The Conser- vatives lost, two seats—Spalding and Coventry,—which were won by Liberals, Mr. Halley Stewart and Mr.. liallantine. In this way the Liberal vote in the House . has been increased from 190 to 200. The Irish Nationalist vote remains unchanged. MR. GLADSTONE'S VISIT TO ITALY.

No Englishman of whatever party who is not abso- lutely blinded by partisan rancour. can fail to follow with peculiar interest the movements of Mr. Gladstone in Italy; and, says a Leeds contemporary, we may be cer- • rain that he will be welcomed with the utmost cordialio wherever he may go hi the dominions of King Humbert. To no Englishman. living or dead, except to , Lord Palmerston, does the triumph of Italian emancipation owe so great a debt as to Mr. Gladstone. His burning denunciation of the nourbon tyranny in the TWO Sicilies contributed in a conspicuous degree towards the development of the profound and earnest sym- pathy in this country with the, cause of Italian freedom, Which waS one of the main sustain- ing forces of the movements that ultimately carried that oanse to ivictory. England did not despatch a single tregiment or more a single ship of war to the assistance of any of the risings by which the hated domination of foreign and native oppressors was assailed and finally overthrown. throughout the Peninsula. Nevertheless, it is undoubtedly the fact that England did render powerful aid to Italy in shaking off the divers yokes that pressed upon her although that aid was confined to moral support. It is that fact which is the explanation of the extremely hearty friendship felt towards this country 'by Italians of all parties—a sentiment the persistence of which has been repeatedly :illustrated in various ways most gratifying to 'English feeling, from the date of the establishment of the Italian Monarchy under Victor Emmanuel down to the present time.

A rumour widely prevailed in Cork on Sunday that Dr. Cross, who is under sentence of death for poisoning his wife, hal made a confession of his guilt, but the Rev Mr. Conolly, Protestant chaplain to the prison, says the rumour is untrue.

• Captain Dunne, Into was committed for trial, in Dublin, on a charge of shooting at the " Reverend " Patrick Higginson White Melville. has been released on bail. The prosecutor has, it is said, gone to Spain, and it is hoped that he will show some trace of patriotism by remaining there. Mr. John Mandeville who was sentenced at Mitohels- town to two months' Imprisonment, under the Crimes Act, for inciting Reston tenants to resist eviction, was discharged from Tullamore Gaol, on Saturday, on com- pleting his sentence. He left at once for Nlitchelstown. His reles,te took Once heinre it WAS expected, and his departure wis scaree:y observed. No representatives of the Nationalist party were present, and consequently there was uo demonstration.

The Premiers's • Jrnistiol has published a correeponti- enee which has passed between the manager of that pa ~t-r (Mr. Gray. M.P.) and Mr. Geschen, arising, mainly, ou .of the latter's speech % at Dublin. Mr. Geschen, in the course of the eorrespotulene, admits that when he was speaking of forged telegrams, his words nnintentionany conveyed the idea that. the Freeman's Journal had been guilty of forgery; end he is sorry in consequence. Mr. Gray taxes Mr. Goschen with vaetteness in the utter- ances in question, thereby ea u..ing the Freeman's journal to fall 'oto certain n•grette.ble On Sunday evening, as Mr. Spaight, J.P., and Mrs. Snaight were being driven in their carriage from killaloe railway station to their seat, Derby Castle, Loughberg, a shot was fired from behind a wall at a point where a bye road turns off the main road. For- tunately the shot. did not take effect on Mr. or Mrs. Spaighf. The bullet however, penetrated the side of one of the team, a valuable roan mare. The utmost in- dienation prevails throughout the district over the incident. Mr. 'Spaight has always been paid his rents • without any trouble. He acquits his tenants, with whom he is on the best of terms, of any connection with the outrage. No arrest has been made. The Land Sub-Commissioners have given judgment in 130 cases on the Kingston estate at Mitchelstown. The aggregala amount ,of the old • rent was £2,470, Griffiths valuation, for Poor-law taxation, was £1,998. and the aggregate reduction by the Sub-Commissioners amounts to about 20 per cent,, of the original rent. The *Phan of Campaign" demanded an all-round reduction of 20 per cent., but an analysis of the revision shows •that in many instances no reduction at all is made. All along the Countess of Kingston was prepared to con- sider each case on its merits, and was actually prepared to give much more advantageous terms than those now settled by the Land Courts, but the National League would not permit the tenants to approach her ladyship. Many tenants are persuaded that I my would have been very much better off had they approached their land lord individually, as the Kingston family were always ready to sympathise with the sufferings of their tenantry. . Mr. Michael Devitt, addressing a meeting of Na- tionalists at Sheepbridge. near Newry, on Monday night. cautioned the farmers agalust availing themselves of the present Land Purchase Act, as he said the leaders of the Irish party had not yet succeeded in bringing the land to its proper value. He advised the farmers to wait until they would be able to purchase from the Government at a nominal rent, 70 or 80 per cent, under the present rents. He declared himself really to follow Mr. O'Brien's example in going to gaol. Leer in the evening Mr. Davin was . presented with an address ie the Home Rule Hall, Newry. There was a good deal rrf "disorder during the proem:Aries, and at one time several of those on and about the platform could barely be re- strained from fighting. Mr. Devitt, replying to an address, said he observed that local differences existed amongst them. The interests of artisan and farmer were alike, for, of course, when all the money that, was now taken out of the country by the landlords was kept ! In it all would be benefited.

div.head: LOVE AND LEARNING.
div.p: LOVE AND LEARNING.

- A well-known,.. elderly nobleman, of large wealth, wooed and won a few years ago, a young and very beautiful girl. Thçir life has been as happy as it is pos- sible for married life to be, when December is united to May. His lordship is distinguished in scientific circles, and possesses high literary attainments. Some time after his marriage he was foolish enough to think that his lovely wife was not sufficiently educated, and laid out a course of reading for her. A. month later he inquired about her progress, and found that she had not opened a book. He set up his eye- brows after the manner of old husbands when their young wives have displeased them. Whereupon she looked up at him with a bewitching smile, and said : I was made to be loved, not to be learned." She won the day, of course. What is learning compared to the light of a sunny blue eye? Would not a husband rather be met with a smile and a kiss, than by a wife who assured him that she "knew her lesson ?" Wisdom is all very well, but winning ways go further. Laughing eyes beat Greek roots all to nothing. A weman's lovely tresses, waving on the outside of her shapely head, are more precious in a husband's eyes than ever so much learning in- side of it. Therefore, all women should endeavour to preserve their attractions, and welcome their liege lords with loving looks, pleasant smiles, and flowing silken tresses, for after all a beautiful head of hair is the crowning charm of a woman, a charm which all may possess by using Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will keep the hair healthy and strong, restore gray or faded hair to its original color, and make it soft, silky, wavy and luxuriant. It may be had of any chemist or perfumer.
