IHOCKING ICE FATALITIES.—GREAt. LOSS OF LIFE. Thew by were skating on a disused clay pit, at Jarrow, on Tuesday, when the ice gave way, and twa were drowned, in spite of efforts to save them. Shortly before noon on Monday three boys, named Prank Devlin, Henry Taylor, eleven years of age. and his younger brother, were sliding and playing upon a lodge of water in the vicinity of Victoria Park, Glossop, the ice being barely an inch thick. Henry Taylor got on to a portion of the ice which let him into the water, and he was drowned, the other boys having narrow escapes. Whilst two lads were sliding on a frozen pond at Daubhill, Bolton, on Monday, the ice gave waV, and both were precipitated into the water. The young- sters made frantic efforts to regain the ice, and, attracted by their screams, a woman hurried to the spot, and threw a clothes-line, by which one of the lads, named Clowes, got out. A passer-by jumped in to rescue the other youth (Leonard Woodvine), and brought him out, hut he died immediately afterwards. On Saturday afternoon, whilst a boy named Willi- vray was skating on Johnston Lock at Garelock, some miles from ellisgow, the ice gave way, and he was pre- cipitated into the water. His mother, who had a stall for the sale of refreshments by the Ride of the lock, rushed in to save her son, but both sank beneath the ice and were drowned without. the possibiNty of assistance reachMg them. A party of curlers witnessed the acci- dent but could render no help. On Sunelav forenoon ParatlPl M`Girr, ten years old, son of John M'Girr, 34, miner, Williatnsburgh, was acci- dentally drowned in the pon4 at. the back of Williams- burgh Wasteworks. An elder brother of the boy had beevi on the pond sliding, when the ice broke, and he fell into the water. Samuel ran to assist him, when the ice gave way where he was standing, and falling into the water alongside his brother the younger one WRS drowned. The elder boy was taken out of the water by Patrick Burns dyer, who had been attracted to the place he cries. The body of Samuel was found two hours afterwards. Two Man DnowtstEn.—On Monday afternoon, a shock; ing double fatality occurred at Rawtenstall. Two young men named Walter Henry Dawson, 17, tinplate worker, of Bank-street, and Peter Hanson, 18, weitver, of Clough- were skating on the New Hall Hey Mill lodge, when the ice gave way, and both were precipitated into the water. Three young men who had Inst. left the lodge heard them call for help, and on looking back saw them struggling in the water and returned, but they were unable to save them. The poor fellows rose to the sur- face and clutched at the ice, but this again broke, and they disappeared to rise no more. Hanson's body was recovered half an hour later, Dawsen's body being brought to the bank about an hour afterwards. On Saturday afternoon a melancholy ice accident occurred on the Rurnfoot or Polketly Reservoir, one of those which supply water to Kilmarnock, and situated about two and a half miles from Fenwick. The accident resulted in the death of William Mather, farmer, Thorn. Fenwick, aged 45 veers: his son, William, aged 11 and his nephew, James, 18 years, son of the }ley. James Mather. assistant minister of Dairy, Galloway. On Friday the farmer bought skates for his son and nephew, and on Saturday afternoon they went to skate. They heel not been long on the reservoir when the ice broke. and the boy fell into the water. The father went to rescue him, and was followed by the nephew. The result was that all three were struggling in the water. The father sank at since, and never came to the surface. The nephew struggled for ten minutes before he suc- cumbed, and his cries were heard a long way off. Another lad, who was also skating on the ice, ran and gave the alarm. The Thorn farm being only some 200 yards distant, a number of persons were speedily on the spot with ropes, but nothing could be done. Two boats were got, and all the bodies were recovered and taken to the farmhouse. Dr. Morris, Fenwiek, was present when the bodies were taken out of the water, but life was ex- tinct. The sad affair caused considerable grief in tle:: neighbourhood.
GENERAL NE'
Mr. Daniel Manninr, late Secretary of the United States Treasury, died on Saturday.

The medical profession of England has lost its eldest member by the death, which occurred on Monday. of Mr. .George Sylvester, of Trowbridge, who was born in March, 1788. He was at one time an assistant surgeon An the navy, and was subsequently appointed one of the Coroners for Wilts, which office he held for 34 years. The extent of the Christmas postal worn in London this year has been so enormous that for the first time on 'record it was found necessary on Friday night, in order to get off the India and China mails, to put on a special late train to Dover. The mails, numbering about 1,000 'bags, wens, despatched by special mail steamer at mid- night from Dover.

TRAGTC AFFRAY TX BIRMTNGHAM.—A fearful affray occurred in Birmingham on Monday. Two police officers went into a house in Loveclay-street to arrest a young rnan for assault. The father of the young man took up a revolver and shot one of the policemen in the jaw, and the son stabbed the other officer in the head. The father was about to fire again uhen he was struck down with a staff. One of the constables is dangerously injured. TRAFALGAR-SQUARF.—No attempt was made by the unemployed, or by those recognised as their leaders, to bold the thrtsatentrl demonstration in Trafalgar-equare on Sunday. About thirty persons collected at four o'clock in the vicinity of St. Martin's Church, and be- haved in a disorderly manner. With this one exception the peace of the district was undisturbed, and the &mare was almost deserted. No special constables were called out.

STEALING A SAFIC—Two men, named John smith and James Keely, were charted before the Manchester Stipen- diary on Monday morning with breaking into a coffee tavern in that city, and stea}ing a safe, On Monday morning the premises in question were found to have been entered (hiring the night and the safe removed. The sate was subsequently discovered in A neighbouring street, but the contents, about £BB, had been abstracted. The prisoners, who were arrested on suspicion, were committed for trial.

PIRP,ON lioArro Star.—On Monday afternoon fire broke out on hoard the ship Navarre. lying in Kingston Dock. Glasgow Harbour. The vessel was laden with esparto grass. The fire brigade was soon in attendance, bui owing to the dense stneke which came from the hold great difficulty was experienced in subduing the flames No fewer than six /if the firemen had to t • convey's,' hemp suffering from the fumes. The flames were under after about an hour's work. Some sixty tons o grass were destroyed. SWUM'S GAq Extunsiow.—An alarming PA exPlO,4" occurred on Monday at the Salvation Army Brirrnel New Bamford. Nottingham. An eseape of gas had how noticed. and the keeper of the premise% William Geory Hainton, Dv-weeded to "1..0k for she leak" with a liO,b• candle. While he was searehing underneath the nls' form the explosion occurred, and Hainton IVRS blew, away, and sustained a fracture of each leg. Five nth ,persons in the roo-n were slightly injured, and all the !windows in the blinding were loown out.

ATTEMPT OF CONVICTS TO ESCAPP.—Under cover of lo ithick fog, two convicts, named Dickson and Wilson. !,bave attempted to escape from the convict establish- ment at Princetown, Devonnort. They were workin on new buildings, and the warder. Robinson, saw them imake off. His guard fired after them, but they were not 'bit. Search parties were then sent out, and a Mr. 'Richards was able to put the pursuers on the right track, be having met the convicts in their flight. Within sari hour and a half the convicts were captured without '.vesiststice. Both men we undergoing five years' penal taervitude. _ _ _

--SitICTDR OF • BANKER'S DATJOHTER.--.on Saturday an Inquest was held at Thrapstone, Northamptonshire, on the body of Amy Caroline Eland, daughter of Mr. R. 'I. Eland, principal partner in a local bank. The deceased, a young lady of prepossessing appearance, locked her- self in a room, and, witha razor, first severed the arteries in each wrist and then cut her throat. The gash in her neck was described by the doctor as being very deep, and sufficient to cause almost instant death. She had lately suffered from religious monomania. The jury re- turned a verdict of "temporary insanity." REMARKABLE CASE or TRANCR.—A strange affair oc- curred at Ditton the other day. An old lady named Thompson has been ill for a considerable period during which she was attended bps doctor. At ten o'clock in The morning she was given up as dead, the doctor taking sway all his instruments, and the family were greatly noset at their bereavement. At about one o'clock pre- iparations were being made for the laying out of the !supposed corpse, when to the great surprise and con- sternation of those present the old lady revived. Mrs. Thompson is, however, still in a very critical condition. I TITRE DISTRAINT ON • CERSTURE CRAPIL.—The • ustees of the Presbyterian Mission Chuveh, Seaeombe. 1 aye received a communication from Messrs. Stephens nd Davies, agents for the rector, Wallasey, Cheshire, manding the payment of tithes. Last year a distraint Ake was affixed to the door, but the matter was not irried further. A notice to distrain has again bee :rved upon the trustees, who distinctly refuse fp reco,g- lee the claim. rho tithe agents have now placed the atter In the hands ef an auctioneer, and ft is said that will vindicate the law by seizing the articles in usein e, church and schools. _

SWOT:UM CHRISTMAS TRAGNDT Hot PARIS.—An at- eropted murder and suicide were committed on Sunday aorning which, from the character of the victim, are of . somewhat serious character. M. Theodore Popel, a bassist' army officer its Paris en leave of absence, became ufficiently enamoured of Jeanne Pierron, a "super "at he Chateau d' Eau Theatre, to offer to marry her. On lday evening, after supping at Sylvain's Cafe, the ,uple adjourned to Flill's Restaurant, in the Boulevard es Capucines. At 7 a.m., after copious libations, they etired to an hotel in the Rue Geoffroy-Marie. There in le presence of a friend of the girl Popel placed two ngs on his mistiess's finger, and called upon God to itness that they were married. This formality accom- ished, he ordered his newly-made wife to prepare to Totnpanv him to Russia. Upon her refusing to accede his desire, he immediately drew a revolver, and fired her three times, wounding., her in the mouth and breast. wing, her fall, as he supposed, mortally wounded, the ussian placed the revolver to his rigl* temple and blew It his brains. Death was instantaneous. The woman

as taken to the Lariboisiere Hospital, and is not ex- ected to survive. FOOT;HARDY USE OF A Pisrot.—At Bolton Police Court, Pri Monday, a youth named Richard Henry Baber was :•hareed with shooting Sarah Rigby, with intent to do her grievous bodily harm. The case for the prosecution was in effect that on Saturday evening a crowd of boys, !including the prisoner, congregated around the shop of ifilrs. Rigby and made such a noise that she proceeded to 'have them removed- As she made her appearance at the dry the prisoner fired a pistol, loaded fortunately ;with blank cartridge, full in her face, inflicting such in- buries that she was rendered unconscious, and had to be placed under medical care. She appeared in the witness 'box with her eves bandaged up, and hearing traces on her face and 'neck of the effects of the charge. The prosecution did not press the case.—The Mayor (Aid. Idoacrop), who was sitting as chairman of the Bench, said it was a mercy something of a more serious nature bad not happened by the foolhardy use of the firearm. 'lie should have liked to have the prisoner flogged, but in consideration of his having been locked up from Satur- day night, and the pleading of bis parents, he would be discharged with a caution, trusting it would boa warn- ing to him and others. The lad, upon whom was found two boxes, one containing powder and the other caps, tainted during the hearing of the ease. • Atraxsue IVIANSLAFORTER NEAR BOLTON.—OrI Saturday ithe police rearrested a carter, named Peter Hreenhalgh, .01 Kersley, on the charge of having caused the death of another carter, named John Will, also of Kersley, who died on Saturday morning from the effects of kicks and bruises inflicted noon him by prisoner some time ag,o Deceased, who had turned 70 years of age, managed to overpower prisoner, who is 30 years his junior, in a wrestle, and prisoner seems to have chafed under the defeat. On the Bth ult, they met in a public-house, iLDC: NW began to chaff prisoner. The ,latter became so ennteed that he knocked Ivill down and kicked hin; abaut the head and OR the body, rendering him mi- coi:soioua. !viii was taken home, and when it was found that he had sustained severe injuries to the breastbone, ribs,head,and other parts of the body, Ivill's depositions ' were taken, and Greenh: was arrested on tho charge of assaulting him and • flir ctin. grievous bodily harm upon him. As Ivill could not attend the court, Green- halal, had to he remanded week by week. After having been in gaol for two or three weeks he was released on hail, but on Saturday, when the police learned that Ivill was dead, they reappreliended Greenhalgh, who will now be charged with the more serious offence- of MB- miauglitßr. EXCITINO FIRE IN LONDON.-.-NARROW ESCAPES.— An exciting scene wrts witnessed in Holyweltstreet Strand. London, on Saturday, by the breaking out of a conflagration, which, before it was quenched, created much damage. The street is very narrow, and the houses old. The flames originated at the shop of a hosier named Ramsay, whose premises back on to a shop in the Strand, which belonged to Leon Serne, where two children were burned to death some time ago, The flames spread rapidly, hut the occupants escaped without injury. Owing to the narrowness of the street seventl shops opposite were ignited, and the terrified inmates escaped to the roof, where they re- mained some time before the spectators below could inducs, them to come down. The shops on each side of Ramset,''s shop, billowing to a picture dealer and book- seller, were also ignited, as well as three shops oppo- site, occupied by a bookseller,a bootmaker, and a picture frame maker. Detachments of the salvage corps and fire brigade soon arridlhd. and is bookseller and about 20 persons were rescued by the former, and placed in safety; while the firemen devoted themstives to preventing the spread of the flames. It did not take long to put out the flames; but not before Mr. Ramsey's premises had been gutted, and the six shops mentioned more or less damaged by fire and water, as well as a ' shop in the Strand, which suffered considerably. A quantity of books, pictures, and hosiery was destroyed, the loss being considerable.

div.head: CHRISTMAS PARTY DROWNED.
div.p: A CHRISTMAS PARTY DROWNED.

A thick gloom was cast over the Christmas festivities at Burnley, on Monday evening, by one of the saddest ice fatalities that has ever occurred in the district. Five persons lost their lives in trying to effect the rescue of each other under circumstances of a painful description, two families in the Gannow district being suddenly plunged into lasting sorrow. Beyond the Tim Bobbin Inn is a large and nearly-triangular disused quarry. known as Tim Bobbin delph, SO yards long and at cer- taM places from 23 to 30 yards deep. The frost of the last day or two had covered the water with a thin layer of ice, which was too tempting to venturesome youths. It appears that at half-past four o'clock in the afternoon, two boys, Frank Hartley, Monmouth- street, and Thos. Hewitson, Zion-terrace, both 12 years of age, were standing by the side of the water. anxious for a little sliding, when Hewitson, to test the bearing power of the ice, stepped on to it, and he purposely jumped to make sure of the strength of the ice, which suddenly broke and let him into the water. Hartley went to his rescue, and neither could get out. On the hank was a boy named Michael Davenport, 14 years of age, of Greenhalgh-street, and, seeing the amiklent, be rushed to the house of Thos. Tattersall, 2, Park-lane, where the five persons, now deceased, were sharing in a Christmas party, and were about to have tea. Their names are Ezra Tattersall, 19 years of age, weaver, son of Thos. Tattersall; his brother, Joseph Tattersall, 17; Arthur Barrett, 19, weaver, cousin of the Tattersalls Joseph Barrett. 44 years of age, father of Arthur Barrett; and John Barrett, 43 years of age, engine- tenter at Maiden Shed, Whittlefield, married man, 44. Junction-street. When they received the alarm they appear to . hftve been panic-struck, and without ant- presence of mind ran along over the hard and lump' gronnd, down the steep sides of the quarry to the edge of the water. One after another they entered the water, each being helpless to effect a rescue and needine assiMance. A person named Alfred Lonsdale, of Gar- stang-street, succeeded in rescuing the two youths. Hartley and Hewitson. Ropes and ladders were imme- diately procured, but the Ave persons in the water ap- peared unable to swim, and they were so benumbed that they amid not grasp the rope that was sent to them. one of the drowning men being heard to say be- fore he sank that he could not lay hold of it, and they all five sank in the sight of persons on the bask who were using every available means to save them. One of thetn, John Barrett, before entering the water, had a rope tied round his arm, but as no one had hold of the other end, it was of no service to him; Joe. Tattersall had a rope fastened round his body, and he appears to have entered without getting anyone from the beak to held him. The appalling loss of life seems due entirely to the excitement of the moment, coupled with the very dangerovs spot where the accident hap- pened. There were loon hundreds of people who gathered along the top of the embankment, 20 yards above the surface of the water at the bottom of a ileei face of jagged rock. Police-sergeant Cant was at once informed of the calamity, and after grappling- irons had been obtained efforts were made to drag out the bodies from each side, and from an extemporised raft, which was immediately made and worked by Mr. James Wilkinson and Mr. Samuel Catlow. One after another the bodies were recovered and carried to their homes, which a few moments before were aglow with h!tppiness. By the strong light of the moon the grapphag contititie& ninch difficulty being experi- enced in recovering the last body, that of Joseph Barrett. The ice-covered water prevented the irons from sinking. hut the moving raft gradually cleared the surface, and at twenty minutes past ten Samuel Catlow got hold of the clothes of the deceased, who was borne throinli the crowd of 'spectators to his home All the men had watches in their pockets, which had stopped at 25 minutes to five. The calamity has taken the life out Of the Christmas rejoicings at all the houses in the locality, and much sympathy is felt for the bereaved relatives. John and Joseph Barrett are brothers, the latter being the father of Arthur Barrett, and uncle to the two Tattersalls. Besides Sergeant Cant, the police who rendered useful service in recovering the bodies were Police-Constables Robinson. Evans, Thwaites. and Holmes; and, in addition to the civilians already named, were Messrs. 9.4. Kenyon and Proctor and others. who assisted the police in every possible way in theii vewreb.

div.head: CHRISTMAS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: CHRISTMAS AT WARRINGTON.

Christmas Day of this year being a Sunday, events of a secular nature held in connection with the fes- tival took place on Monday. On Sunday, however, services of a special nature were held in several of the churches of the town, and these places of worship were as a rule suitably decorated. The I kindly gift of the Mayor of a dinner to a large num- ber of the poor of the town also took place on Sun- day, at the Drill Hall. Monday was almost gener- ' all observed as a holiday by the townspeople. The two football matches which were played on the ground of the Warrington Football Club during the num- ber of h holiday omu ai egetn seekers, enday,treatedoA f t each the day proved to be great attractions to a large mthousands.aspectatorste swer e tihinne match countedaathe Ito their annual dinner, as were also the scholars at saPelawndtagya occasion st eaiiii tdauhslttelai time Schoolbarrack ari itra thee n ko roomsT barracks,sd w 3,. and-ere,e n aat Christmashue spuraeils-, elaborately decorated. A substantial and season- , able dinner was partaken of by the soldiers on I Monday, and in the evening there was dancing and other modes of enjoyment indulged in. Below we give cl,tailed reports of the various events. DINNER TO THE WORKHOUSE INMATES. The usual Christmas dinner was given to the inmates of Warrington Workhouse on Monday. Dinner was I 'Served to 142 men, 77 women and 28 children in the large dining hall, while in the hospital 58 woman, 53 men, 18 inArin females' and 15 infirm males and a num- ber of children partook of the repast. The fare consisted of roast beef, plum pudding, and beer or coffeeaceording to preference, and was excellently prepared and served I I under the superintendence of the Master and Matron 1 (Mr. and Mrs. Ward). The members of the Board of IGuardians present were Mr. W. Darbyshire, Mr. G. ytat-i eliffe, Mr. R. Isherwood, and Mr. T. Jolley. There werel also present among others, Mr. J. Smethurst, Mr. and the Misses McCollom, Mr. S. E. Hopkins, 8.A., and Mr. Greenway. The rooms were prettily decorated with plants sent by Sir G.Greenall,M.P. andMr.Lvon. After dinner Mr. JOLLEY, who was received with cheers, said he was glad to be with them once more, to wish them "A happy Christmas," and to see them enjoy themselves so thoroughly. A good dinner had been provided by the master and matron, and he was sure they would give them a hearty vote of thanks for their kindness (cheers.) The plum pudding was really excellent, for he hadtasted it. They had also enjoyed their beef and beer, and he hoped they would show that they appreciated the efforts of the Guardians and other friends who had come amongst them that day. (Applause.) On an occasion like the present all distinctions of society should be levelled. They were all brothers and sisters at Christ- mas time, and there should be "Peace on earth and good-will to 'men." (Applause.)—Three cheers having been given for the Master and Matron, Mr. WARD, in reply, said that was the first Christmas dinner at which he had had the pleasure of spoaking to them. On. his own behalf and that of Mrs. Ward and the other officers of the institution, he thanked them for the appreciation of the labour which had been expended in the prepara- tion of the dinner. The Board of Guardians had very generously provided them with a substantial dinner, to- gether with some plum pudding of the quality of which none of them could grumble, and a pint of beer each, and he thought they ought to feel very much indebted to the Guardians present. (Cheers.)—Three cheers were then given for the Guardians.—Mr. DARMYSIIIItE, in reply, said the Guardians came to the Union every fort- night, and some of them oftener, to do their best for the inmates of the house, and the Cheers which had been given for them would be appreciated. It might be that some of the Guardians looked upon their welfare in one light and some in another—some temporally and some spiritually—but they wished altogether to enhance their happiness here and to prepare them as far as they could for the happiness of the life to come. (Applause.) There was not a member of the Board who had not their wel- fare at heart. (Cheers.)—Mr. James SJIETHCRST, in re- turning thanks for the visitors, :41icl they were all sisters and brothers, both at this and other seasons of the year. He thanked them very cordially indeed for the kind manner in which the vote of thanks had been passed to the visitors. After a reference to the dinner in the Drill Hall on the previous day, Mr. Smethurst expressed a hope that the poor would look upon that house and other houses of a similar character throughout Englandp not as a workhouse, but as a house of comfort which they all in their days of prosperity had helped to support by the payment of rates and taxes. (Cheers.)—The rest Of the day was spent by the inmates in a suitable manner. PADGATE INDCSTRIAL SCHOOLS. At the radgate Industrial School Christmas was cele- brated in the customary seasonable manner by a dinner on Tuesday. The children in the school number 200- 120 boys and BO girls—and each of them was supplied with roast beef and plum pudding, and afterwards with nuts, oranges, &c. The room in which the repast was served was very handsomely decorated, the work having been dons under the directions of the superintendent and matron (Mr. and Mrs. Mines). Amongst the visitors present were Mr. W. Derbyshire, Mr. J. Houghton, and Mr. W. Houghton, members of the Board of Guardians; Mrs. John Houghton, Mrs. Woods, and Miss Whittier; and Dr. Peacock° (medical officer of health). After din- ner, Mr. Minns said they could not separate without showing their appreciation of the goodness of those who had provided such substantial fare for them, namely, the ratepayers of Warrington and the Warrington Board of

Guardians, (Applause.) He was sure they had all had a good dinner—it was quite equal to those which had been given in previous years. Mr. Derbyshire had al., ways taken a great interest in the welfare of the chil- dren, and if he had not come amongst them that day they would have begun to wonder whether they were . I having their annual dinner or not. (Hear, hear, and' applause.) He was also glad to see present Mr. John •! I Houghton, Mr. William Houghton, affd Dr. Peacocke, as I well as a number of ladies who had kindly assisted the - officers of the institution in waiting upon the children during dinner. In conclusion' he asked them to give < three hearty cheers for the Guarclians,—The request was t responded to in a hearty manner, three cheers also - I being given for the decorators.—Mr. DARIITSRII2E, in re- I tUrning thanks on behalf of the, Guardians, expressed the pleasure it afforded him to see the room so handsomely decorated, and the children looking so well. He wishea tb impress this fact upon the children—that their charac- ters should be so formed in that school that they would never require the support of the ratepayers when they left it. The great object for which these schools had been erected was to train up the children to make themselves self-supporting during life, so that they might become honest and in. industrious citizens, and not be made; the necessity of sending their own children to this •schosl to be educated. (Applause.) In conclusion, Mr. Derbyshire said the thanks of the children were due to Mr. and Mrs. Mines for the kind way in which they treated them. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. Wm. HonormoN, in a few remarks, said he hoped the children would profit by what had been said to them with reference to their conduct in the future, and that when they left the institution they would never be under the necessity of returning to it. It would be a great gratification to the Guardians if they found that , this proved to be the case. (Hear, hear, and applause.) --Cheers were also given for Mr. and Mrs. Mines and family and Dr. Peacocke.—Dr PRACOCKE, in returning. 1 thanks, said he had had many opportunities of visiting - institutions of a similar character to that, but he had never seen such a number of fine-looking and healthy children as he then saw before him. (Applause.) He should always endeavour to do his duty to them faith- fully. (Applause.)—The rest of the day was spent in an enjoyable manner. - DINNER TO THE POOR. At noon on Christmas Day about 1,200 poor people , . were supplied with a substantial dinner, which was' served in the Drill Hall, at the expense of the Mayor (Alderman T. Sutton.) The tickets had been entrusted for distribution to Mr. George Riley, School Attendance Officer, and they were given to the deserving poor of- both sexes, of all ages, those present ranging in age from six to over sixty years. The viands supplied them —hotpot and rice pudding—were cooked by Mrs Booth, and were of an appetising character. The scene in the ; Drill Hall during the progress of the meal was an inter. eating, though to some extent a sad one. It was plain that the guests 'were heartily enjoying themselves, but • the pinched and careworn appearance of many, even of the little children, was such as to strike an observer very forcibly. However, all present seemed to make a hearty meal, and to enjoy it thoroughly. During the progress of the repast the members of St. Paul's choir sang Christmas carols and glees. Among the ladies and gentlemen who gave assistance in looking after the wants of the guests, in addition to the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs Sutton), who took a very active part, were the Bev. S., Mrs, and Miss Wilkinson, Councillor John Prierpoint, Mrs Pierpoint, Mr. Thomas Morris, Councillor J. E. Wright, Mrs Harrison, Miss At- kinson, Mr. and Mrs Morton, Mr. Charles Madeley, and Mrs and the Misses Smethurst, Messrs. J. H. Sme- thurst, John Griffiths, T. Pilkington, H. Sutton, W. Sutton H. Cookson, the Misses Geddes, Mr. G. Anton,' Miss Sutton, Messrs. C. Bunch, John Glover, Rowe, Peter Chrimes, Miss Chrimes, Miss Garland, and Mr. Joseph Gernard. Towards the close of the dinner one of the men present briefly proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor and Mayoress or their hospitality, and the Mayor in reply, wished all present a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. As the children left the room they were each presented with an orange, and the married people had bread given them to take home.

CHRISTMAS AT THE BARRACKS. The military stationed at Orford Barracks kept up- Christmas on Monday, when the men dined together in their respective rooms. In the evening dancing parties were formed, and there was vary general enjoyment. The various barrack-rooms were tastefully decorated., the work having been carried out by the 7ollowing Liverpool Regiment :"A Company, Colour-Sergeant Jack- son and Sergeant Barnard B Company, Sergeant Stacey and Private Jones; C Company, Private Bewley; D Company, Sergeant Naylor and Private Callaghan. South Lancashire Regiment: A Company, Private Con- nor and Drummer Mulchy ; B Company., Sergeant Aug.; tin; C Company, Privates Smith and Riley; and D Company, Privates Turner, Gibson, Macdonald, Smitli, and Swallow. The followpig are a few of the mottoes in the rooms of the Liverpool Regiment: "Our best wishes to+Major Graham," "Long life to Colonel Twentyman, C. 8., his wife, and family, • "Prosperity to Major Joce- lyn," "Success to Major Ritchie, his wife, and family," "Success to Lieutenant Farrar," "Success to Lieutenant Harris," " Success to Lieutenant Clarke," "Success to to the non-commissioned officers of B Company," "Suc- cess to Sergeant-Major Simpson," and "Long life and prosmity to the officers of the 8-40 R.D.;" whilst arnottgst the honours which were displayed maybe men- tioned Delhi, Oudenarde, Afghanistan, Malplaquet. Ramillies. Burmah, Lucknow, and Powar Kital. The mottoes in the rooms of the South Lancashire Regiment included—" To our Sergeant-Major," "The Liverpool Regiment," "Compliments of the season to Captain Kellie," "Health to Lieutenant Thompson," •` A merry Christmas to Colonel Twentyman, C.B.' and family," "Success to Lieutenant "Barrow," "A merry Christmas to Major Linton," "Luck to our Navy," • A long and successful career to Lieutenant Barrow," "A happy and merry Christmas to the Colour-Sergeant and family," "Long life to Major Ritchie ;" and the honours included the following :—Salamanca, Cabool, Orthes, Vittoria, Sevastopol, Lucknow, Waterloo, Toulouse, Candahar, and Nivelle. TREAT AT THE RAGGED SCHOOL. The children of the Warrington Ragged School had a Christmas treat on Monday. To the number of 420 they flocked in from all quarters, some without shoes or stockings, and most of them scantily clad. To each child was given a bag containing a bun, scone, and cur- rant and plain bread. About fifty children who could not enter the room were supplied with food outside. A pleasant evening was spent in singing, and cheer# were given for the superintendent, teachers, and friends, who so willingly waited upon the youngsters with tea; and for the tradespeople who had so liberally supplied the bread. Each child was presented with an orange on leaving the room. The teachers desire to express their sincere thanks to all those who have assisted them, and also appeal to all benevolent people for clothing, books, &c.

GLADSTONE, while on his way to Italy, for. the rest L:nd recreation to -which he is so much en- titled, delivered an address at Dover, on Tuesday, which is calculated to set a-thinking politicians of every shade. It was not confined, as many of his speeches have been, to the Irish question; but was a survey and a review which shows at every turn that the leader of the Liberal party is up to every move of the politic:al game. There is no evidence in his speech of the decline of that natural force which is so indecently anticipated by his enemies. On the contrary, the signs ara innumerable that Mr. GLADSTONE is, intellectually, as eager and pis powerful as he was half a century *ago. We know that he carries the burden of seventy-,eight years; but the speech is, as to tone and vigour, the speech of a man who is in his. prime. It is exhilarating to see "the old man eloquent" lead the way into the thick of the fight with all the ardour of youth; and he is hardly worth 'calling a .Liberal who is not isiimillated to prove himself in sonic degree worthy -of so glortoug f!. iqaditr. There 1194 been a good deal-said, in the absence of any other excuse, about the Liberals having been the cause of the barren- ness of the last session of Parliament; but, as Mr. GLADSTONE shows, the . Tories Owe it to their own incapacity that the time of the House was wasted. They crippled freedom of debate by new rules of procedure, and, as if that were not enough, they seized the nights of private members, thus .robbing Parliament of its independent voice. Purther, they set about putting shackles upon Ireland, and when Ireland resisted, as she has always resisted, they blamed other people for wasting time which they had themselves misused. The one bright feature hi their dark career is their foreign policy; the Ministry seem, so far as we are able to judge, to. have followed in the path marked out for them by their predecessors; and Mr. GLADSTONE, with char- acteristic generosity, does not hesitate to say that, with such-lmowleclge of the situation as he can command, he approves of the course which has been taken. It is in home matters that the Government have neglected their opportunities, and seem likely to neglect them. What hope is there for the future, when it is proposed that there

shall be 'a repetition Of the blunder of last year by frittering away the earliest and best part of the session in framing stringent rules of procedurd? This is a trick for killing time and punishing the Opposition which may be played once too often. The people of this country want to see something done; they are getting impatient of this inter- minable discussion of rules •for considering what shall be done. Local government reform was pro- mised by the Tories when they were seeking office more than two years ago. It was urged that it was a matter which they were prepared to deal with immediately; but so far as can be gathered they are not even yet prepared to open the next ses- sion with the long-promised measure. It is inti. mated that it will ba introduced after Easter, which means, as Mr. GLADSTONE puts it, that the

bill is simply to be dangled before the country, 'and that there is no intention of passing it into law. It is the threadbare policy of masterly in- activity, which some peOple have been sanguine enough to think would be set aside when the Liberal Unionists were as spun; to prick the sides Of Ministerial intent. But Tories would not be Tories if they were Reformers. Coming to the Irish question, it becomes obvi- ous that the leader of the Liberal party is in goad heart with the progress which the Home Rule movement is making. He remembers that the Liberal party has never yet inscribed upon its banner the name of a cause without carrying its

----- banner to victory; and how can he doubt that it will be the same with Home Rule, when majori- • ties in Ireland, Scotland, and Wales have declared for it, while bye-elections indicate that What was the minority in England has in all likelihood grown into a majority ? Lord SALISBURY may attempt to palm off his romances of Irish history as something true as hely writ; but when Mr. GLADSTONE is on his track there is not the slighest hope that the Imposition will make headway. People now-a- days keep their eyes open, and although they still admire the juggler, when he has the cleverness of the PRIME MINISTER, they understand pretty well "How its done." Lord SALISBURY lets it be understood that he has set himself to the task of etting-rid of "the unnumbered horrors of chaos and disorder;" and his theory is that this is .to be accomplished by disregarding the national senti- ment of Ireland. Consolidation is to be aCconi- plished.by coercion—just as butter is obtained by coercing .cieara. • His lordship has the idea that the Irishinam is to be made happy by sitting on his chest. There is not the least evidence that Paddy likes the operation; the fact is, it causes him to rebel because it makes him miserable. The ilalisnury theory is that the remedy has failed because it has not been applied continuously; if the Irishman can only be hold down for ever he will become peaceable and contented. And so Ire- land is to be consolidated by coercion. Was there ever such arrant nonsense? Coidd the force of folly further go? Lord SALISBURY would eternise the bungling of eighty-seven years, and call it wis- dom. Mr. GLADSTONB seeks to profit by experi- ence, and rink° Ireland happy by making her fr6e. . •

The people of Wales seem determined to profit by the example of the people of Ireland; they are forming a Land League with a view to the rafGrin of the land laws, and, if the new organisa- tion is supported in the Principality as it is ex- Peeted it will be, it will certainly have far-reach- ing consequences. Its' strict title is "The. Welsh Land, Commercial,. and Labaui League,"—a
WiAUM

bersome designation which will doubtless he I shortened for general use to "The Welsh Land League." It is stated that the Liberal press in Wales regard the manifesto which has been issued by the new Association as the most important that has been, seen for many years. Its pro- gramme is 'undoubtedly a inost Radical one, but Wales is a ICa.dical country. The objects of the League are fourfold;—" To secure (1) a fair basis for the imposition of tithes and continued support to those who may be subjected to legal process for the non-payment of tithes; ,(2) the disestablish- went and disendownient of the English 'Church in Wales and ' the transfer of its endowments to national purposes; (3) refesrais of the laws which relate to land, building leases; royalties. on coals and minerals, the game laws, the .rivera, and all other laws relating to laud which are prejudicial to the interests of the country at large'; (4) the retura to Parliament of Members who understand, the neeis of farmers and of the labouring classes, such members to be paid from the national fund." These are objects which, it is not at all unlikely, will commend themselves' to - the bulk of the Liberals of Wales; lut it remains to be seen -whether, when it comes to a question of details, it may nothe found that an attempt is being made to corer too muth with one net. The Welsh are hard set just now as to the tithes question, and it would be absurd to ignore this vital issue in any scheme of reform 'drawn up specially in the inter- ests of the Principality. None the-legs it is pos- sible that there may be diffsrences of opinion amongst Welshmen as to what constitutes "a fair basisfor the imposition of tithes." It is a subject, of course, which interests English farmers, who not unnaturally complain whorl a linsd tithe is imposed whether the season be good or bad. The most elementary ideas of justice would suggest that when the farmer has had a bad year—when he has lost money after twelve months of toilsome work—it is not fair that he should be tithed to the support of the Church just as if he had had a year of plenty. If a tenth of the produce were literally taken, it is obvious that the portion set aside towards the maintenance of the chrgy would vary with varying years. And this is what should obtain, if it can be satisfactorily arranged. There are some who talk about abolishing the payment of tithe in a rude and sunimary fashion; but this, while it would for a time relieve the farmer, would be an immediate injustice to the Church and a final robbery of the nation. For it must be re- membered that tithes in so far as they are Church property an llAlOnal property,. and the time will arrive When the nation will set about devoting a great portion of the money to other and better uses than those to which it is at present applied. Farmers would benefit very little in the long run by the unconditional abolition of tithes. If there were no tithes to pay, "the higgling of the mar- ket" would cause rents to rise, and the difference would finally find its'way in to the landlord's pocket. The farmer would have gained little or nothing, and the nation would have lost the title to the control of a vast yearly sum. It is due to the promoters of the Welsh Land League to say that they are not insensible to the difficulties of the situation. It is suggested that tithes should be paid on a 'sliding sale, the hasis of which should be the prices of the previous year, This would undoubtedly be an improvement upon a seven years' average, for if it did happen that the tithes of a good year should be paid during a bad year, there would be some rectification of the .anomaly during the year following. Lord SALIS- BURY is professedly anxious to settle the tithes question; it is to be hoped, therefore, that he will give this proposal the attention it deserves. He will assuredly find that it will not be a satisfactory settlement to arrange that payment shall be made to the landlord instead of the clergyman—the basis being practically left, untouched. With regard to the suggestion that, when the English Church in Wales is disestablished and disendowed, a portion of the proceeds should be devoted to education, elementary, intermediate, and technical, we cannot but think that it is one which will meet with favour not only in. Wales, but with approval as a proposal which would be applicable to the rest .of Great Britain. There will be a great outcry against it_ by the Church party
but that is to be expected as a matter of course. There is not much danger,that the Church will be badly 'treated, when it comes to a legislative
division of the loaves an fishes; arid as to the

Clergy, they will be fully capable, as they were in Ireland, of taking care of themselves. With regard to the other chief object of the Land League—the Reforni of the Land Laws—we would remark that judging from the manifesto, there is a risk of
„ getting too little done' by attempting too much. Tories as well as Liberals are pledged to great changes; and it is needful, unquestionably, that every phase of the land question should be well
_ discussed. Coming to the last point—the pay- ment of members by the League--,we must con- fess to some doubt as to whether it will be carried

out on any considerable scale; but it will be some- thing to be prond of if the Welsh combine to send half-a-dozen paid representatives to Parliament. They are, at any rate, in earnest, and they are resolute; they are in the van, and we bid them God speed in the path of reform.

Mr. Gladstone was 78 years of ageoh Thuriday. A long, long life to 'him, and more pOwer te his elbow!
St. Paul's Cathedral is to be. cleanca. It is to be washed once a century whether it wants it or not. There is nothing like having a rule in these

The Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar of St. John the Baidist Church, Earlestovin, seems to be on better terms with his congregation than he was a year or two ego. • He was presented, on Monday eVening, with a silk hood and stole. "It's never •too late to mend."

' One of our contemporaries reproduces the obituary notices of people who have died during the past year. This may be eheerfuf Christmas reading, but wouldn't an• account of the year's births and marriages be more " german to the mat- ter?" We do not at Christmas, after all, celebrate the death of Christ.

Miss Louise Imogen Guiney, the American poetess, has been receiving honours in her own country. She went into a shop the other day .to order firewood; and when she gave her name the entranced shopman clasped his -hands in ecstacy and exelaimed--0 Oh, Imogen 1" There, now, that is much better than "Whoa Emma!"

The Committee that has been inquiring into agricultural and dairy schools has reported in favour of district schools, to which a Government grant should be given. A Central Normal School is also recommended, which would become a sort of , College of Agriculture. Pupils who wished could "go from the District School to the Central School. This is technical education as applied to farming, and it cannot be too soon brought into operation

Mr. Henry Greenall has received a nice little Christmas present—he has been appointed clerk to the Daresbury ' magistrates. His father and his brother-in-law were on the bench when the appoint- ment was made—there is nothing like having a friend in court. Mr. H. B. White, who was act- ing as deputy-clerk, would doubtWza think he had the first claim; but it does not appear that he had any relatives on the bench; and what is the use of having reletivo if they d not oblige you?

- The poor we have always with us, and it is satisfactory to note that they are not overlooked in Warrington and other places at Christmastide. The Mayors of Warrington and St. Helens divide "the cake," or, shall we say, .come under the mistletoe? this year for their benevolence. Alder- man Sutton (Warrington) gave a substantial din- ner to about 1,200 persons on Christmas Day; and Alderman Maechnie (St. Helens), has ar- ranged to present 1,250 hotpots on New Year's Day.

We are improving somewhat in our ways of enjoying Christmas. The younger generation know at any rate how to seek intellectual recreation; but there is still a vast number whose only idea of having "a good time" is in getting intoxi- cated. This is shocking in a man, but doubly shocking in a woman. What a sad picture it is— that of the Widnes woman who set out in a tipsy condition, on Saturday night, to find her way to another. ; and was ultimately herself found lying dead in Ditton Brook

Christmas festivities In a good, many places have been marred by fatal ice accidents. It would ap- pear that the irregular frosts we have had this sea- son, affording as they do so little opportunity of skating, have Made people 'anxious to try the ponds the moment it was thought they might bear. The result is an appalling series of disasters. ,It is difficult to enforce, e lesson in these cases; but parents will do well, with the younger members of their families, to see to it by their vigilance that the risks are reduced to a minimum.

The experiment of giving . penny dinners to school children is meeting with considerable success, especially where it is conducted on a toler- ably large scale. In winter, especially, children must have a good meal in the middle of the day, if they are to be fit for afternoon Study. Would it not be possible by-the-bye, to give the girls prac- tical lessons ix-Abe art of preparing these dinners? Familiarity with the cooking a penny dinners during their schogl-days might save them pounds in after life.

The Tories are " gentlemen " as Mr. Chamber- lain would say, and it was the pink of politeness on the part of the Tory gentlemen of Dover to organise that reception of Mr. Gladstone on Tues- day, which was characterised by snowballing, hiss- ing, and the braying of brass bands. These gentle- men, however, seem to have been harking back to their ancestors. Serpents and geese hiss; but why a brass band? They might surely have shown themselves to the manner born by braying without one.

The Rev. Dr. Aird thinks that the destitute crofters of Lewis have a right to rebel when men arecompelled,to starve on the land in order that wild animals may fatten. It may be said that this is dangerous doctrine; but what is rebellion? And is there no rebelion that can be justified? It is a far cry to Lewis, and these men must raise their voices, if they would be heard. And no great harm either, if by a little wholesome resistance they bring it home to sporting landlords that they are of more moment than a herd of deer. ,

We had occasion to remark• the other day that Prize-fighter Sullivan patronised the Prince of Wales when H.R.H. interviewed him. This is the Bruiser's opinion of the Prince, according to the "Chicago Tribune" :—" He is a nice, sociable fel- low," said the slogger, "with splendid manners, and, taking into consideration all that he has had to fight against in the way of family, a splendid, good, all-round man. He is the sort of a man you like to meet anywhere, and at any time, and intro- duce your family to." Really, now, this is very pretty—especially for the Prince.

The Rev. Jacob Primmer seems to have been "letting off" on Christmas Day. HI said Queen's subjects were absolved from their alle- giance because her Majesty had been "running after Popish priests, monks, and nuns." As for the Pope himself, he was "flown at" as "the greatest imposter, tyrant, and blasphemer on earth." This is bad language," coming from a minister. Ordinary mortals are sometimes brought before the magistrates for" cursing and swearing '." and it would be interesting to know whether the Rev. Jacob Primmer could not be "run in" under the same law..

Mr. Gladstone, in his speech on Tuesday, pointed out that the Tories were not to be trusted on the question of Protection. It would be a sur- prise to many that he pointed to a danger from the Irish members. He said—" Our cencauTence with them is simply a concurrence of public opinion on matters on which we are agreed, and if the Irish Nationalists choose to vote for Protection; we have no fault to find with them." Mr. Gladstone has not forgotten that when they were negotiating with Lord Carnarvon, they stipulated that power should be given them, under a Tory Home Rule scheme, to set up a protective tariff.

, Sir James Fergusson, Under Secretary for 1 Foreign Affairs, speaking at Dalrymple, on Tues- day, said "He was inclined to think that Ireland was a country which wanted governing with a good tight hand, and not a country in which a mere majority could be entrusted with the .power of ruling the whole." This is an honest, straightfor- ward way of putting the ease for the Govern- ment; it is good old-fashioned Toryism. Majori- ties must not rule ;" they must be ruled. What is the use of troubling to give local self-govern- ment to "Hottentots" or "tWe swinish multi- tude "—to use an older phrase? Give ' them bullets and bayonets if they will not submit to the minority: .

A number of • the subscribers were present, and supported the Vicar on theplatform. IKE VICAR or FARNWORTH "SOLD Up." Consider- able .commotion was caused in the usually quiet village of Farnworth, near Widnes, on Thursday, by the sale -of the .household effects and library of the hey, George Bond, M.A., vicar of Farnworth. The fact that Mr, Thomas Worthington, the sheriff's officer, Was officiat- ing as auctioneer under several writs for large amounts gave rise to much gossip. . The living, which has been held by Mr. Bond, for about eight years' is in the gift of the vicar of Prescot, and in the Clergy List is stated to be worth £650 per annum. On Monday, the prisoner, who was accom- panied by a woman, applied for lodgings at the prose- eutor'sliouSe. He was rdfused admittance and went away. fit a later hour the men met' each other in the street, and without receiving any provocation whatever the prisoner knocked the pbpsecutor to. the ground and kicked Ifin several times upon the head. SiiOT IZOI3LATtIES AT RuNcoßN.—Yesterday, at RIDICOTTI Police Court, before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. James Handley,Marr,aret Frances McKeown, a married woman, ' of Canal-street,.was brought up on remand charged with haying s'ailen a coat, value £l, the property of Harriett Dodd, clothier, Church-street. Tno coat was missed from the shop door on Saturday evening, and the same night the ntismier rercived lOs upon the article from Marsh and Smith, pawnbrokers. Inspector Millington afterwares apprehended the woman, win alleged the coat belonged to her hosband, bat afterwards said a woman gave her a 'glass of whiskey to pledge it. The prisoner was also charged with steal;rg four shawls, the property of Mush and Smith, pawnbrokers, Church-street. . The shawls ' had been missed at different times, and when Inspector Mill'ngton apprehended the prisoner on the ptevious charge he found in her pbsseasion pawntickets. relating to the missing at eicle.s. Three shawls had been deposited with Wil'iam Craddock, pawnbroker, and one with E. Imison, pawnbroker.—The prisoner informed the Bench that she had committed the robberies " through a drop of drink and company."—She was sentenced to two Months' hard labour—a month on each charge. MURDEROUS ATTACK Wilt A TABLE KNIFE AT RUNCORN. —On Wednesday, at Runcorn Police Court, Thomas King, a' labourer, was charged on remand with having on the. 19th December unlawfully wounded Martin Gilligan, also a labourer. Gilligan, it appeared, was an inmate of Gibson's lodging house, in Mersey-street, and the prisoner had lived there for the past six weeks. On Monday evening the 19th, about six o'clock Gilligan was sitting in the kitchen when the prisoner entered. The men had been on good terms with each other, and the customary salutation of " How Go" was exchanged, Mrs. ;dartha Farrell, also a lodger, inquired of Gilligan what time he would get up in the morning and he re- plied " From five to half-past, I am not same as some " men Who go to a "pub." and swagger that they are in time enough' if they get up at nine o'clock." The , prisoner retorted by calling Gilligan a liar," and picking Up an ordinary table knife which he was using at the thrfe, the prisoner aimed a blow at Gilligan, Gilligan warded off the blow with his left hand, which was cut in the operation but before he could make his escape the prisoner had Plunged the weapon into his left cheek. The blade also penetrated the tongue, and caused two wounds of a dangerous character. The in- jured man was subsequentlytakerr to the surgery of Dr. McDougall, who dressed the wounds, and at a later period P.C. Dutton took the prisoner into custody, at the house. The Constable asked which was the knife that the deed was done with, and the prisoner taking up the table knife (produced) said "this is the knife."— , These facts having been proved the Bench committed the prisoner to Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial. A CHRISTMAS Ent SATURNALIA AT DITTON.—At the Blackburn Arms, Dittonon Thursday, Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquest on the body of Eliza- beth Taylor, who was found dead in Ditton Brook on Monday. Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, represented the relatives. Fk.Taylor, lalcourer,of 42, Charlotte-street, said the deceased' was his wife, and was 50 years of age. He last saw her alive at half-past eleven on Saturday morn- ing, when he went to his work. She was then sober. He knew she,had tickets for a raffle at the New Inn, hut she promised she would not go. A labourer named John Wilson had lodged with him since April. When he came home from his work on Senday, aborit 8-45, he ascer- taine i that his wife was missing. John Wilson told him that he left his (witness's) wife on the road; and he did not know where ahe *as. Wilson's father, who was present, began blackguarding him. John Wilson then said, "It is all right ; I know where .I can put my hand upon her ; " but after- wards he said he aid not know where she was, and explained "We were coming along Ditton-road arm in arm, and we both. fell down. I put her on her feet and' she ran away from me." Witness admitted that.his wife was sometimes addicted to drink.—By Sergeant Rosa: He WS told his wife was forward in drilk when she left Widnes.—By Mr. Knowles: His wife always carried a purse, and on Saturday, after paying for her groceries, she woald have about 14s with her, Neither purse nor money was found upon her.—John Wilson, who was cau- tioned, said he was a nightsoil labourer, and lodged with Taylor. On Saturday night he went with the dc. ceasel and Mr. and Mrs. Penrungton by the 6 pan. train ' from Widnes to Bitten. They went straight to the New Inn, kept by. Julia Hannah Miller. They left about a quarter past ten, The raffle took placein aprivate house. . Mr., and Mrs. Pennington left first. He and Mrs. Taylor followed, and after going about eighty yards along the road they both fell down. He got up as well as, he could and put her onher feet. He then went to Lees, at the Railway Hotel, and got a pint of ale in a bottle. He afterwards met John Clay in Ditton- road. He (witness) fell several times and Clay took him lion-e which he reached about twelve o'clock. By Ser- geantßoss: Both he and Mrs Taylor were drunk when they came to the New Inn. ,He had three or four pints there. A quart of whiskey was on the table and he took it home. Pennington told him Mrs Taylor had paid for , it. He did not remember being ordered off the railway companies premises at 11-15.—As there were several bruises and cuts upon the body of the deceased, and the , evidence was not altogether satisfactory, the coroner adjourned the inquiry until Tuesday in order that a post mortem examination might be made.

Before Mr. Brundrit, at Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Peer Stobo, a hawker of jewellery, hailing from Liver- pool, was charged in conjunction with John Williams, a collier, from Hanley, Staffordshire, with stealing six pairs of trousers, the property of Arthur Davies, pawn- broker, High-street, on the ,28th inst. Prisoners were furthec 'charged with having stolen a half-gallon tin bottle, the property of John Dutton, tinplate worker, of Devonshire-square, on the same date.. Prisoners were apprehended by Sergeant Woolley and P.C. Da/e, and on being charged made no reply. Each of the prisoners were wearing a pair of the stolen trousers, and the bottle was found at a lod3ing-house. Two 'pairs of trousers were discovered wrapped up in a bundle in the same nlice, and one pair in a bedroom, whilst the other pair had been pledged at Mr. Craddock's pawnshop.—Pri- soners were remanded for a week. ' A DISCHARORD SOLDIER AND HIS WlFE.—it the Chester. City Police Court, on Friday morning, before General Ineall and Messrs. C. Townshend and T. Q, Roberts, William Didsbury, a recently-discharged soldier from the Cheghire Regiment, and residing 'at Weston, near Run- corn, appenred in answer to a summons charging him with an assault upon his wife, Mary. Prosecutrix de- posed that she had only been married nine months, and had, in consequence of 11C7 husband's ill-treatment, left him upon two occasions. However, they :came to Ches- ter last Saterday to spend the Christmas with *le friends at the Castle, and he had been ill-using her ever' since. When near the Castle-yard he knocked her crown insensible, saying he would tale her life. Defendant ad- mitl-ad striking his wife, but pleaded provocation. The Bench said it was ve 7 sad to see defendant, after only a few month's married life, behavine himself in such a manner—lt wakrnost cowardly of him to strike her, and espeelally more so when he WaSlcdiseharged soldier. He would be bound over to keep the peace for slx months towards his wife, himself in £2O and two sureties of LIO each, and pay the costs, or go to prisen for seven d'vs. CHPISTMAS AT DUT'IYIN WORICHOUSE.—The imitates at Dutton Workhouse were plelsantly reminded of Christ- mas as early as five bkdock on Christmas morning, by the boys and girls shrine 'carols in the corridors and wards, and each inmate received a Christmas card at /real-fast. In the more serious case Mr. Blower, an assistant master et the Middlewich National Schools, was going home from Sandbach, when he was knocked flown, robbed of .£3O, and then carried to, the canal and flung in. lie had a. narrow escape of his life. THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION.—On Tuesday sta- tistics were issued announcing the progress during the past year of this Union. There arr 4,500 churches in England and Wales. against 4,460 last year. The ministers number nearly 2,700, seven have left the denomination, and three others joined. Sitting accommodation is provided for 1,600,000 people. Scotland has 100 churches and Ireland 29. In Great Britain and the Colonies there are 18 colleges. with nearly 500 students. The London Missionary Society is training 300 native students. 'LORD COMPTON ON PROTECTION.—Lord Compton, presiding at the annual meeting of the Yardley Hastings (Northamptonshire) Co-operative Society, said that without intending to make a political speech he should like to take the opportunity—is fact, he intended to take every opportunity—of Protesting at the top of his voice against the hideous doctrine that was being preached through the land, and preached by people who ought to know better, that hideous doctrine which was given the very pretty name of "Fair Trade." It, 'was the wish of those who urged that question to send up the prices of certain things; whereas the conten- tion, he hoped. of all co-operators was that it was for their benefit to get their things as cheaply as possible Me entreated all who were interested in the question to study, not only those economic laws which regulated England's fiscal system. but also those which regulated the production and the sending slut ,of goods. They would thon clearly see that it was for the advantage of the country to have our ports open to the world. A llBAnmass nernun.—A man named George Cameron, a baker by trade, who is employed at St. Helene, was brought before two magistrates at the Borough Court, on Thursday. on a charge of having. in May last, left his two children to be maintained at the cost of the parish. FrOin a statement made by Mr. Shearer, who prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Guardians, it appoared that prisoner, just, after completing a sentence of fourteen days' im- prisonment for deserting his children. endeavoured to make some arrangement with reference to them, and promised to take them out of the Workhouse , within a certain time. Instead of doing so, he went ' to America, and, returning to this country, was ap- prehended. Mr. Shearer added that it seemed to be the deliberate intention of the prisoner to get rid of the children, for on one occasion he left them in the streets, . The case had cost the Union .£l5 17s, independent of prosecution expenses. It was men- tioned that prisoner, in addition to serving it fort- night's imprisonment as previously stated, had also been sent' to prison for three months for the same offence, and he was now again committed to hard labour for a like period.

THZ FATB OF NourawicH.—ln the course of an address at a banquet on Thursday night of the Salt Chamber of Commerce, at Northwich, Mr. Falk, the president, said they exported three hundred million tons of salt annually to India, and it would shortly be increased to six hundred million tons. No (13- vernment dare raise the duty on salt in India. He defied the Government to do it, and he told Lord Cross so to his face. It would agitate India from one end to the other. Corning to the question of subsidences at Northwich, Mr. Falk said that por- tion of North wich on which they were standing was doomed, and the people had better migrate. (Laugh- ter.) He told them now, as he told them four years ago, that Northwich was doomed. They would presently have a great ravine running across Castle Hill and Witton-street. Leftwich would be as safe as a rock. Why not migrate there? . - COUNTY PRESENTATIOL—On Thursday, at an ad- journed annual session of county magistrates, held at Preston, Lord Derby, the chairman, presented to Mr. Jacson, chairman of the General Finance Com- mittee, on behalf of the county justices, his por- trait, painted by Mr. Sydney Hodges, London. In highly eulogistic terms his lordship referred to Mr. Jacson's long connection with, and strong personal I interest in, the business of the county. Mr. Jacson suitablyteplied. The portrait is life size, and will be hung in the County Hall. The business. of the Court was then proceeded with. The reports of committees were presented, the assessments for the ensuing half-year were decided upon, and the to- port of tl.e County analyst accepted. The estimates of funds required by the treasurer to tarry en the expenditure of the county from the quarter ended 30th November, 1887, to the end of August, 1388, was submitted to the court. It included the police rates, the rate for Warrington being ld in the to raise .£1,549 7s. Superintendent Barker, of Present, and Superintendent Johnston, of Widnes, were ap- pointed inspectors of weights and measures. On the recommendation of the Chief Constable, the tnwnshipfe of fold. Cron ton, Dit ton, Hale, Halewood, Rainliill„SPeke, and Widnes, and the' •municipal borough of St. Helens, were formed into a Weights and measures district, to be called .the Widnes dis- trict., the distinguishing mark on the stamps of such district to be 107 with the crown over.

THE luau QttssrzoN —The following letter has .been addressed , to Mr. Mcllwaine, Knowsley, who, it will be remembered, wrote two valuable letters which appeared in our columns a few weeks ago : " dear Mcllwaine,—Excuse me for not sooner replying to your kindness in sending me the papers containing your valuable letters. ' You corld not do a work :ofqreater charity or patriotism than expose the Tory policy of..M.P.'s and others, who take ad- vantage—as they have always done--of the religi- : ous prejudices of. the Protestants of the North of Ireland, as to .thie may be justly attributed the very existence of the Tory party in this country; and to them the greater part of the poverty, rioting, and ' bloodshed for generations oast, as by this means they have managed to maintain a sort 'of religious warfare, for the purpose of keeping the People divided, and thereby screen themselves from the concession of the 'just demands of what would have otherwise been a contented, law-abiding, and united people. You have, to my mind, struck the nail On the head at every stroke, in the points which you have treated in your lengthened letter, and consider it a great hardship yon did not Send it for insertion to the "Perry Journal" and other Liberal papers of the North of Ireland, or ask them to copy. Of course, I am unable to give an oPiniOn as to your suggestion of a Home Rule schOme, but have no doubt it might work well. I. have availed Myself of the only means at my disposal of giving it circulation, viz., by reading them and giving them to be read at Plumridge and other _faces where there were a number of people of everfifineraination congre- gated for the purpose of paying rates, and all ad- mitted their truthfulness and expressed their pride and satisfaction that you had the qualities, and particularly that you had the courage, being a Protestant of the North of Ireland,' as such a letter from an English Liberal—if he were capable of .writing such—or even from the pen of Mr. Glad- stong himself, would be of little or no value in comparison. Wishing you and Mrs. Mcllwaine and family a merry Christirias and happy New Year, be- lieve me, yours truly, CHAS. MCLOUGHLAN, Kells;N. Stewart, to. Tyrone. •

(hon. secretary). The fourth annual reportof the directorswas presented as follows :—" The directors be, to report that they re- elected Mr. T. Sutton Timmis as president, Mr. R. H. Davies as vice-president, and the Revs. T, Finegan, J. Wright-Williams, Messrs. Deacon, Handley, and Timmis as the . Executive Committee for the fourth year. A chance in the system of prizes and certificates was deci- ded upon by your directors, the object aimed at being to increase the number of third class prize winners lov ' additions from among those children who had not previ- ously gained prizes. By the scheme now in force, each prize winner gains a deposit* of as. This increase is evidently due to some exient to a migration from the second class, as the numbers in that class have fallen from 584 to 528; but it is also due to an increase from below. The Chairman moved the adoption of the report, a ad remarked thatk the primary objects of the Council va ire to encourage good attendance at school, and to aid in forming thrifty habits amongst the children. It wa a very gratifying to know that these objects had been at - tamed in a very great degree, and it would be a great pity if the usefulness of the Council was to be impaired through lack of funds. As to the scholarships given to Farnworth (hammer School the parentsof oneof the suc- cessful boys was in a good position and very honour- ably did not apply for it, but they took the book grant:. M. Jones seconded the motion and 'the report was adopted. r The retiringdirectors were re-elected, and Mr F. H. GO*. sage was re-appointed honorary treasurer, and Mr. Dea- conM 11. Deacon °ll.s'r etary. Mr. remarked that if the scheme was to be carried on next year it would be necessary to get more money some how or other. _ The Chairman said the Council had done a great deaf of good. Mr. Williams as a school manager would endorse that statement. The Rev. Wright Williams: Yes. Mr. Davies said subscriptions were received from a rnero fraction of the population, and if the Council had more funds they could enlarge the work very materially., They, raig,ht pay the fees of those children :who had passed the sixth standard. CHRISTMASTIDE AT RUNCORN AND • WIDNES.

The great festival of the Christian Church was ob- served much in the same way as in former years. On Christmas Eve the youths and those attaining to man'a estate, appeared to have an "extension of time." Up to a late 'lour they patrolled the streets in groups, and in a 'more noisy than harmonious manner expressed their feel- ings with regard to the occasion. There was a considerable number of those who had wor- shipped Bacchus not wisely but too well to be seen in the streets, but as will be seen from the "black lists" at the police courts, the interference of the police was necessary in very few instances. Shortly after midnight the streets were comparatively quiet, and numerous companies of carol singers were to be heard discoursing strains of vocal harmony of the world's Redeemer. On Christ- mas . Day the weather - was far from .Season- able. In the .morning a drizzling rain fell with provoking persistency, but during the after- noon. the sky cleared somewhat, and the night was bright with moonlight. Being Sunday the custom- ary services were held, but the various pastors re- ferred in appropriate terms to the occasion. The clutrches, and most of the chapels, were decorated with ivy and holly in profuse quantities. Monday was regarded as a holiday by the tradesmen, but the numerous chemical and other works were in full operation, and the working people generally had to don the fustian. The traffic on the railway was, nevertheless, very heavy. Liverpool, it the numbers are a guide, was the most popular resort, although Manchester was visited by many. In con- sequence of the football matches at Warrington, special trains were run to • that town, and they were taken advantage of by many hundreds.

• FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS AT PENBETH. • Yesterday, an inquest was held at the Black Horse Inn, Sankey Bridges, by Mr. Brighouse, coroner, touching the death of Frederick John •Roughley, who died from injuries received from a fall down some cellar stairs at the Crown Inn, Pen- keth, on Monday.—Mr. J. G. Roughley, landlord of the Black Horse Inn, Sankey Bridges, said the deceased.was his brother, and had lived with him. He was a flint glass cutter, and was 28 years of age. On Monday morning he left home about eleven o'clock to go to a sparrow " shoot "at Penketh. About half-past two in the afternoon he was brought back suffering from injuries. Drs. Shermtt and Itichmond,were Sought, but deceased died at 6-30 p.m. the same day. He was con- Brims when brought home, but he did not say how he came by his injuries.—Harry Child, a young man, who lives at Hud-lane, Great Sankey, said he knew the de- ceased, and saw him about ten minutes to sae o'clock in a Yield at Penketh, where there was a sparrow "shoot" going on. About half-past one o'clock witness .and the deceased, along with others, went to the Crown Inn. The first room that they went into was so crowded that they could not get sitting room, and he called to deceased to go into another room.. In going along the lobby into which the cellar door opened, he went before deceased, and he heard the latter say, "Let's ko in here," and before he could speak to him de- ceased fell. Witness went on, not knowing that deceased was hurt, and did not see him again till he was taken into the yard, when he seemed to be badly hurt. He ac- companied deceased home in a cart, but did not hear him say how he happened to fall. There was no disturbance or quarrel of any kind in the lobby at the time deceased fell.—James Jackson, landlord of the Crown Inn, Pen- keth, said he newer saw deceased in his house till he saw him at the bottom of the cellar stairs. On entering the house he heard his wife say that she thought some one had fallen down the cellar steps, and he went there and found deceased, who was unconscious. His (witness's) opinion was that deceased thought the cellar door led into a room, and fell when he was stepping in. There had been no quarrelling in the house, and he had heard nothing to lead him to think that anybody had pushed deceased downstairs. There had been no previous acci- dent at the stairs. although to his knowledge the house ; had been a public-house for 30 years.—A verdict of "Ac cidental death" *as returned, and the jury made a pre sentment to the effect that some steps should be taken b the owners of the Crown Inn ta remove or alter the e- trance to the cella", as they considered .that in present condition it was dangerous to people using t house.

A FEW CANDID FACTS.

Every careful observer who has sought to keep Dace with the march of events, has noted the alarming increase of certain peculiar physical troubles within the past few years. These troubles have come at unexpected moments and in a most treacherous way. They have manifested themselves in innumerable forms, but they have always had the same cause. They have not afflicted the minor parts of the 'body, but have gone direct to the strongholds of the system and their work has usually been as prompt as it is fatal. Their treacherous and deceptive nature has often preven- ted a careful analysis of what causes them, and, as a result, intense suffering and final disaster have usually ensued. The real cause, however, has been a derangement of the kidneys and all of these troubles are, in fact, the first symptoms of the terrible Bright's disease, which has cast it dark shadow over so many homes in the land and is increasing wonderfully and con- tinually. It is now conceded by the ablest physicians in -every land and by eminent scientists the world over, that this disease is the result of blood poisoning.. This poison- ing is brought about by wasted and unhealthy kidneys that permit the poison to remain in the blood, instead of throwing it from the system. To purify a stream we must go to its source, and to cure a disease we must re- move the ;cause. It being true, that nine-tenths of all human ailments are caused by diseaded kidneys orliver, the only certain way to cure these troubles is by treat- in" the organs which cause them. How intimately the kidneys are associated with the entire system may be understood from the fact that over 1,000 ounces of blood pass through them every hour, being more than 200 gal- • lons or nearly one ton in the course of twenty-four hours. This vast mass of living fluid is sent to every part of the body, and if the kidneys are diseased the impurities that are in the blood are not removed, and hencepassthroutgh the veins, tarrying disease in some one of its many terrible forms. The horrors which accompany most of the diseases caused by disordered kidneys and liver can- not be described in print, while the dangers surrounding them are even greater than the agony. And yet a per- son may be troubled for months without knowing the cause of the diseases that have attacked him. Some of the symptoms of the first stages, any one of which indi- cates disordered kidneys or liter are these: Pains in the back and around the loins, severe headaches, dizzi- ness, inflamed eyes, a coated tongue and a dry mouth, loss of appetite, chilly sensations, indigestion (the stomach never is in order when the kidney-s:or liver are deranged), a dryness of the skin, nervousness, night sweats, muscular debility, despondency, a tired feel- ing, especially at night, puffing or bloating under the eyes, Sze. The above are a few of the hundreds of symptoms which indicate the beginning of aggravated cases of kid- ney or liver difficulties, and they require instant atten- tion. If these symptoms are not checked at once, they are almost certain to result in some one of the many ter- rible diseases of the kidneys. But unpleasant as all the symptoms and even these diseases may be they are as nothing compared to the last stages of the.com-

plaints. There is but one known remedy that has ever been able to cure serious kidney troubles or control those great organs when once deranged, and that remedy is Warner's Safe Cure. The test of merit is in what has been accompliiihed, and knowing of cures almost num- berless in England, Canada, and the United States, many of theth chronic and given up as incurable, makes us bold to say in all sincerity that for all diseases of the kidneys, liver, and urinary organs, Warners's Safe Cure stands alone; not only in point of excellence, but in the wonderful results it has achieved. The remedy can be had of all chemists at 4s. 6d. per bottle.

It was stated by the complainant that he heard the dis- charge of a gun, and afterwards saw two of the pigeons drop, the other being wounded, and on going to where the gun had been fired he saw the defendants with guns in their possession.—On the other han& the defendants admitted having been out with guns on the day in ques- tion, but denied that they had ever shot at or even seen any pigeons.—The Chairman remarked that the case was a suspicious one, but on the evidence the Bench could only dismiss the summons.
