div.head: WARRINGTON PEOPLE'S COLLEGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON PEOPLE'S COLLEGE.
The following are reports on this school, made by H.M. Inspector, which were read at the recent con- cert given by the pupils, and which were crowded out of our last issue :

SEX KIR Saroot.—The work of this large school continues to be carried on with the same zeal and efficiency as here- tofore, both teachers and scholars being animated with remarkable enthusiasm and earnestness over their work. The tone continues irreproachable, and the discipline, with the exception of some inclination on the part of the older scholars to talk when unemployed, is highly satis- factory, and deserves special mention in the first and fifth standards. Reading in the whole of the first standard, and the second standard (girls), spelling in the third standard, composition in the fifth and sixth standards, and the whole of the class work, are points that may be singled 'out as worthy of special commenda- tion. Clan the other hand, there is some weakness in the fourth standard, much of the reading being halting and stumbling, the spelling not up to the level of what is found elsewhere, and the number of problems in arith- metic worked successfully being below the mark. Hand- writing throughout has received careful attention, and singing by note in the highest division continues to be thoroughly well prepared. In a large and important school like this instruction in practical cookery would be of the greatest benefit. A better arid more eves set of pupil teachers papers I have never seen. All the pupil teachers, namely, Arthur Knowles, Joseph A. Bunch, Sarah Sowards, Annie H. Ashurst, Emily Brown, Amy A. Plinston, Mary Williams, and Mary A. Seward' have passed well. Mr. Hall, Miss Twiss, and Miss Dig- num will receive their certificates in due CAOUTAB. BANK QUAY INFANTS' BRITISH SCHOOL.—This mho* maintains its excellent condition in discipline and in struction alike. The work is carried on with energy and good methods, and the results are very satisfactory. The reading throughout deserves praise, especially that of the first class. Writing, spelling, and arithmetic are also very good, and the children are bright and intelligent in answering on object lessons. There has been a good variety of exercises and occupations. Miss Isherwood will receive her certificate in due course.

CAIRO-STREET INFANT SCHOOL.—This department is well and kindly conducted, and the instruction in the elementary subjects has received careful attettentiot, and is, generally speaking, good. The reading has im- proved, and is now in a very satisfactory condition, both as to expression and intelligence. Spelling is but fairly accurate. Mental arithmetic, however, is ready and well prepared. The discipline in the second class rnlob be rather more close and Ilrm, and habits of atteetton better established. The pupil teachers—Ada Wright and Eda A. Pickton—have passed well.

the place. Dewsbury continued to press the cheesernen, and Graham again got hold, and with a fine left-leg drop sent the oval over the doss-bar. After this Runcorn had a look in, and Gatley and Faulkner headed a dribble in the home 25, where Hughes essayed a, drop at goal, which was near coming off. Lockwood pluckily ran the ball out, and the finest exhibition of passing throughout the match now took place between the Runcorn backs. Hughes, Cawley, Speakman, and Davies each handling the leather, but it was of no avail, the tackling of the Dewsburyites being too secure,and only a minor rasulted. Darkness was now approaching. and time was shortly afterwards called, leaving the home team winners of a pleasant and fast game by two goals, ,three tries, and one minor to one minor., ,Teams:—Rtmcorn : Brazen- dale, full back • Cawley, H, Speakman, and T. Davies, threequarter backs; H. Hughes (captain), and H. Andrews, half backs; W. Faulkner, Broady, G. Wain- wright, J. Galley, J. Barns, Gaytes. Ran, Clarke, and Dolan, forwards. Dewsbury: Lockwood, full back; Hopkins, Stewart, and Graham, threequarter backs; Sampson and Stadden, half backs; Gee, Beck, Redfern, Lorryman, Wolstenholme (captain), Leather, Wilman. Jackson, and C. Garforth, forwards. WARRINGTON V. OLDHAM (A Teams).—The Warring- ton "A " team journeyed to Oldham, on Saturday, to play their first fixture with the Oldham " A " .team. The Warrington team was not a very strong one, whilst the home players had evidently got together as strong a team as they possibly could, having obtained the assistance of several players from local clubs. The field was also in very bad condition, being ankle deep in slush, and par- tially covered with snow. The home captain won the toss, and Whittle kicked off for Warrington at 3-30 against the wind and hill. Scholes returned to Evans,, who got in a good kick, play settling down in the home quarters. Antrobus got nicely away, the ball going into touch in the Oldham 25. Good passing between the Warrington backs took place, but Mather was collared by Clough before he could get away. The ball was next dribbled to the home full back, who kicked to Evans,' this player making a very good attempt at goal, a minor resulting. Buckley dropped out; Warburton saving near centre. The Warringtonians worked the ball to the Old- ham goal line, where Whittle got possession and passed to Evans. this player transferring to Warburton, who dropped at goal, but the desired point could not be effected, the ball going wide by a few feet, another minor point being the result, Buckley dropped out, Evans making a good return. Mather next got in a good kick to Fowler. who returned well to Jolley, who failed to gather the ball (it being very greasy) ; and it was drib- bled over the line, but the Warringtonian full back managed to drop on the ball, a minor only being regis- tered for Oldham. Warrington next forced their oppo- nents on to the goal line, but Harrop got the ball away nicely by a kick, Jolley sending the leather into touch. The visiting forwards, headed by Adamson, Craghan, Eves, and Molyneux, again dribbled to the home line, where Whittle passed to Evans, but he was promptly collared by Buckley. Unsworth headed a rush to the Oldham line, a try appearing certain, hut unfortunately Thornley stepped on the ball when in the act of dribbling, and it bounded back, thus enabling one of the Oldham forwards to get the ball away by a kick to centre. Play now raged in midfield, when, from a loose scrimmage, Jones kicked across to Mather: but the latter player was charged off the ball by Mayers, and Buckley kicked to Jolley, the ball rebounding off this player into the hands of Buckley. who had no difficulty in grounding the ball near the line, no goal resulting from the place kick. Half-time was now called, with the score standing—War- rington 2 minors, to Oldham 1 try and 1 minor. Potter re-started, Evans returning to centre. Antrobus got away from a scrimmage and passed to Mather, who got in a good kick. A good dribble by Unsworth forced the home team to touch down. Antrobus returned the drop out, Adamson preventing any return being made. Warrington now forced their opponents on the defensive, but the home full back got the ball nicely away to cen- tre. Whittle next passed to Antrobus, who throw to Warburton, who kicked well, Clough returning into touch. Craghan was next conspicuous by a dashing dribble, Mardis* saving. Whittle now obtained a free kick in front of goal, Warburton taking the plane kick, but nothing came of it, and Mayers returned to centr, The Oldham forwards broke away and forced the ball over the Warrington goal line, atouchdown being scored. Unsworth was instrumental in taking play to the home quarter flag, Fowler saving well. Time was nowcalled. the score standing—Warrington. 3 minors; Oldham, 1 try and 2 minors. Teams: Warrington—Full back, Jolley: three-quarter backs, Warburton, Evans, and Mather; half backs, Whittle and Antrobus; forwards, Craghan, Molyneux, Adamson, Eyes, Thornley, Jones, Bate, Unsworth, and Donohue. Oldham—Full back, Fowler; three-quarter backs, Mayers, Buckley, and Clough ; half backs, Lowo and Ha,rrop ; forwards, Potter, Chapman, Murdock, Gomersall, Scholes, Milhaud), Sjx- smith, Criles. and Mellor. wEsT LANCASHIRE JUNIOR CUP COMPETITION— FINAL TIE.

WOODMAN ROVERS v. WIDNES RECREATION. The final contest for the possession of the handsome cup presented as a prize to junior clubs by the West Lancashire Rugby Football Union,took place on lSonday 'last on the commodious ground of the Warrington club, off Wilderspool Causeway. The two competing teams were Woodman (Wigan) Revere and Widnes Re- creation, but a slight hitch was caused at the commence- ment by the appearance on the ground, irr football cos- tume, of Scot-lane club, who alleged that they had not been properly beaten by the Recreation in a previous tie. It appeared that the decision had been given in favour of the Recreation elub in accordance with rulers, and, con- sequently, the Scot-lane contingent were removed from 1 the scene of play, though they displayed a very large amount of reluctance to forego their claim. There was a very large attendance of spectators, both teams hav- ing evidently been accompanied by a large body of fol- lowers. The game was started by Grundy on behalf of ' the Widnesians, but owing to off.side play a scrimmage was formed on the centre line, and the Rovers quickly displayed a superiority in the forward department by carrying the ball into the Widnes quarters. These efferta were, however, eontemcted by Broome, who made a fine run and kick. Widnes were again checked in the scrim- mare, and Halliwell gained gronnd for the Revera. The Widnee men responded by rushing the ball to the Revere' line, but Topping secured and made a smart run along the line, and brought play to centre. The Rovers now began to evince a decided superiority, and from a scrimmage near the Widnes goal the ball was transferred to Barton, , who neatly dropped a goal. After this success the Rovers played with more dash than ever, and still main- taining their fine combination they penned the chemicals within their 25. The latter, however, played a plucky defensive game, but the passing of their backs was ex- tremely injudicious. Nothing further, however, was scored before change of ends, at which time the Rovers were leading by a goal to nil. In the second half the Wicinesiane still manifested the same pluck and determi- nation in playing a losing game, bat their combination was if anything more defective than ever. As a consequence they rarely succeeded in getting much be- yond their 25. Their backs were at. times singularly careless in parting with the leather when near their line, but as the Rovers were rather slow in taking advantage of the opportunities given them they only succeeded in in increasing their score by a. try (Dickenson) and a minor. The game thus ended in a win for the Rorer by a goal, a try and a minor agahtet nil. Speaking generally the Rovers undoubtedly owed their victory to their superior discipline and combination as they played to each other's hands in a very effective way. On the other hand, though several of the Widnea men showed that they were made of excellent material, as a whole they seriously lacked unity and consequently the efforts that were made were fragmentary and ill-supported. The following were the teams :—Woodman Rovers : .1. Top- ping, back; Yates, J. Barton. and W. Taylor, three- quarter backs; E. Dickenson and Halliwell, half backs; J. Denson (captain), J. Taylor, W. Collier, J. Seddon, Marden, J. Bithell, T. Farrimond, J. Dowling, and J. Houghton, forwards. Widnes Recreation: D. M'Cririe, back; R. Broom, R. GrundN-, and W. Braelehaw, three- quarter backs ; J. Smith and H. Barber, half backs; T. Wailing, H. Hewitt, J. Trinkies, A. Robinson, H. Dain- tith, R. Charles, J. Passy, J. Johnson, and E. Dickson, forwards. Umpires, Messrs. Wilcock and Barnes. Referee, Mr. R. Beewick, Swinton. After the game Mr. F. T. Parry, the secretary of the West Lancashire Union, requested the President of the Warrington Club (Councillor W. Pierpoiet) to. present the trophy to the winning team. In complying with this request, Mr. Pierpoint. rot/wed that it had been said that cup competiti ens were at to raise ill-feeling between clubs and consequently that they conduced to rough play. This. impression ho thought, however, had been shown to be unfounded by the game they had witnessed that day, which had been played in a very gentlemanly man- ner. (Applause).—The presentation flaying been acknow- ledge on behalf of the victors, the large gathering dis- persed with cheers for the competing teams Sre. WARRINGTON V. OLDHAM.

The first of the annual matches of the above clubSwas brought to a close at the Wildorspool enclosure on Satur- day, before a fair attendance of spectators. Several of the usual players were away from both sides, Massey, Fair. Turner, Davies, and Rigby being alcoeht from the Warrington side, whilst Barlow and Wood were away from the Oldham ranks. Two 30's having been agreed on, Armstrong started, Ashton charging the kick-off down, and the first scrim- mage was formed in Oldham territory. A pass from Mills to Wrigley was intercepted by Barnes, bat directly after Johnson made "his mark," but Nevins safely piloted the loather back into the Oldham 25. Ashton, Littlewood, and Holland dribbled to the line, but Wright got the leather away in the nick of time. 'The play was very even, until a kick by lialkyard momentarily in- vaded the Warrington 25; but the homo team forwards, headed by W. Dillon, pressed the Oldham men back. Bandies now shone with a neat run, and Jolley almost got over after a strong run. Halkyard and Armstrong relieved to the quarter-flag but Barnes retaliated by a tricky run to the lines. quarter-flag, saved a dangerous rush, and Wrigley relieved the pressure by a timely kick to midfield. A good rush by Turner and Ashton took the leather over the line, Johnson saving by kicking dead. The drop out found the " wirepullers " again in the Old- ham •25, but after some give and play which followed Barnes secured possession, and dodging in miraculous style, evaded all the backs with the exception of Pulla- love,. and taking his drop at goal missed, but Appleton was m attendance and safely grounded. Loud cheers

greeted this effoit, but Speakman failed to add the pre- mier point. Appleton returned the drop out, and smart following up by Lees prevented Nevins returning a. kick by Wrigley. Barnes now got in another tricky run, and the 'visitors were again forced to concede a minor. The home team hid the best of the tame from now to the call of half time, the score then ;ading—Warrington, 1 try and 2 minors ; Oldham, 1 minor. Barnes recom- menced hostilities from the centre, a poor return being made. Bandies got over after some loose play, but on appeal this was disallowed. Halkyard "made his mark" and relieved to midfield, but the relief was 8114 Y temPorary, for Warren by a grand effort took the leather to the line, an unlucky pass forward spoiling a certain chance of scoring. Barnes was again applauded for some tricky work, but the Warrington forwards, who played a grand combined game all through, rushed the. leather to the line, Fullalove saving. Jolley was cheered for a flue run, and almost got in, but SUCPA”.I was met with by Barnes securing possession on the stand side, and, dodging his opponents, got over cleat to the corner flag on the Wilderspool side. This was a brilliant run, and Frank Turner almost did the needful. Turner by a huge kick again threatened the visitors' goal, but Fulls.' love got the leather away, only to see it well returned by Nevins. Warren and Barnes put in some sterling work here, but the climax was reached when .Tolley secured posseesion, and scattering his opponents in all directions grounded beneath the posts. Itindeed reminded one of his efforte at Dewsbury, and on emerging from tlie thick helves the reeipient of much applause. Barnes took the place, and kicked a neat goal. Armstrong re- started, and for the first time in the second half the Old- ham men invaded the Warrington 25, and a rush by the visitors over the line ended in Halkyard scoring. The place was too difficult for the same player to intrease its value. Barnes dropped out, and Oldham played up with increased vigour. Lees, Mills, and Ingham headed a dribble; but Appleton ran the leather back to eentre. No other point was now scored, and when the whistle was blown for no-side, the Warringtonians retired vic- torious, after a pleasantly-contested game; by 1 goal, 2 tries, and 3 minors to 1 try and 1 minor. ' The combination of' the home team was perfection, and, Without doubt, was the finest exhibition of the Rugby code that has been seen on this ground this sea, son. To credit any single player would be an injustice, for one and all played their level best. On the Oldham side, Mills, Halkyard, Johnson, and Armstrong ware the pick of a splendid team. The following were the teams :.—Warrington: Full back, Navies; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes (cap- tain), Appleton; half backs, Warren and Speakman; forwards, Ashton, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, Fovey, Little- wood, Hayes, Frank Turner, Bandies and Holland. Oldham: Full back, Fullalove ; three-quarter backs, Wright, Wrigley, Johnson; half backs, Mills and Hol- den; forwards, Armstrong (captain), Ripley, Halkyard, Ingham, Lees, Bromley, Welstencroft, Mallalieu, and Nuttall. Umpires, Messrs. Gilbert and Court. Referee, ,Mr. G. W. Vickers, Salford P.C. WARRINGTON V. WIGAN.

The Last of this season's fixtures of the above clubs was brought off on the Wilderspool ground on Monday. A large crowd of holiday seekers was in attendance, it be- ing estimated that close on 6,000 spectators would be presert. It will be remembered that in the first of these matches Warrington journeyed to Wigan with rather an indifferent team, and consequently had to pay the pen- alty, suffering defeat by two tries. On the present oc- casion Warrington were able to put a representative team into the field, although Massey, Fair. Turner. and Rigby were absent. On behalf of Wigan they received the assistance of Roberta and Lawson, of Leigh, and Dempsey, of Aspull, and with such valuable acquisitions it was naturally thought a gallant bid for victory would be made by each opposing team. - Two thirties having been agreed on Wigan kicked off, and the visitors playing with great dash soon forced two minors. This reverse seemed to rouse the home team, for, on the second time of re-starting, they quickly in- vaded Wigan territory. Warren was the first to show with a smart tackle of Samuels, and a kick by Appleton to Slevin forced the game at the Wigan quarter flag. Abbott was here collared with the leather in his posses- sion, and, from the Jinn out, Speakman got over, but this was disallowed. The Wigan man relieved their , lines grandly, but the Warringtonians, not to be denied, again took the play on the Wigan lines. Hayes saved a dangerous rtisli hero, and Jolley made his mark, but Prank Turner failed to utilize it, and, after much give and-take play, the leather was found in neutral ground. W. Dillon put in a smart dribble to the Wigan 25, and Appleton was next conspiuous by saving a rush of the visiting forwards. The next item to notice was a splen- did combined dribble by the Warrington forwards, this smart piece of play completely dumbfounding their op- ponents. The game rested on the Wigan line, and after some pretty passing by Warren, Barnes, and Jolley, Davies got over under the posts. Barnes' kick struck the uprights, no goal being registered. From the drop- out, exchange kicking by Appleton, Nevins, and Abbott took place, the play being confined to neutral ground. The Warrington forwards pulled themselves together for another effort, with the result that Frank Turner was enabled to score a try, Barnes again failing. This was only the forerunner to another success, for soon after the recommencement, Ashton from a line-out gave Barnes a chance, that player lowering the Wigan goal. One goal and two tries in such a short space of time was indeed marvellous, and after start- ing again from the centre, the Wigan men could not withstand the continued onslaught of the Warrington- ians, but luckily for them half-time was called with no addition to the score already mentitoned. Frank Turner commenced the second half, and aghin the grand combi- nation of the home team told its tale, Bandies, Jolley, Speakman, and Barnes showing to great advantage. Warren passed smartly to Barnes, who in turn trans- ferred to Jolley, that player making a strong bid for scoring. The visitors now rallied; but Lacked the dash which was so prominent in the first few minutes. They invaded the Warrington 25, but it was only temporary, for a neat pass from Warren to Barnes again forced the game on the Wigan lines. Speakman, who saved the rushee of the Wigan forwards time after time in marvel- lous fashion, was applauded here for some sterling play. Exchange kicking by Barnes, Abbott, and Nevins ended with interest to Warrington, and after a splendid exhi- bition by the Warrington backs Frank Turner crossed the line, but on appeal this was disallowed. Littlewood was next conspicuous by scoring but this was served in a similar fashion to the one previous, and Jolley directly Afterwards had hard lines in not scoring. Nothing of interest was now noticed except a good run by Bandies, and a certain chance of scoring was spoiled by picking up. In the end, however, the Warringtonians won a hard-fought match by one goal, two tries, one minor, to two minors. The Warrington team deserve the greatest credit for their display of,Monday last. Their combination was simply perfection, and they well deserved the hearty plaudits that awaited them at the close of the match. Individual praise cannot be given, as all played a ster- ling game. On behalf of Wigan,' Slovin Wardle, Law- son, Atkinson, and Dempsey were the 'NOMA :—Warrington: Full back, Neyins ; three- quarter-backs, Apppleton, Barnes (captain), and Jolley ; half-backs, Warren and Speakman; forwards, Ashton,. Frank Turner, W. Dillon, Davies, Povey,Hayes, Bandies, Jones, and Littlowood. Wigan: Full back, Abbott • three-quarter-backs, Samuels, Slevin (captain), and Roberts; half-backs, Lawson and Wardle; forwards, Atkinson. Carrington, Hall, Yates, McCamm, "Robin- son," Jackson Dempsey, Hutton, and Clegg. Referee, Mr. Hall, Oldham Football Club.

L&TCHFORD 110IINETS v. SUNLIGHT RA.NOBILS. - This return fixture was played off on Monday on the ground of the former, and ended in a win for the home team by 2 tries and 3 minors to 1 minor:

RUNCORN FRSB WANDERRIIS (IST TRAM) V. All the visitors played a good and combined game, and for thehome team, Hughes, Hough, Shaw, Jones, and Handles were the pick. Winless • ST. UELIIINS.—This fixture was decided at St. Helens, on Saturday, before a large number of spec- tators. Neither team was fully represented, and a game of two thirties was played. Widnee won the toss, and elected to play with the slope, and St. Helens kicked off. ,IThe visitors' forwards, headed by Hardman, rushed the ball splendidly to the home quarters, where Parkinson secured, possession, and dashed over the line in brilliant style, but on account of knock-on play the point was not allowed. Subsequently Morris, from a neat pass by Par- kinson, dropped at goal, but only a minor resulted. Give-and-take play , followed, and ultimately, from a scrimmage, Parkinson secured the leather, and dropped a beautiful goal. At half-time the score was—Widnes one goal and three minona to St. Helens one minor. The second half was more evenly contested, but, despite their strenuous exertions to score, St. Helens were unable to do so. Parkinson passed to Wilkinson, who gained a beautiful try, which Morris failed to improve, and after evenly-contested play, the game ended in a victory for the visitors by one goal, one try, and five minors to three minors. Farrell, `Parkinson, Wilkinson, Hardman, Kiddie, Woods, and Barber played well for the visitors, whilst Eastham, Halton, Liptrot, and M`Loughlin were the pick of the home team. Teams--Widnes S Bing- ham back • 9 Morris, J Parkinson, and R Barker, three- qua;ter.bacias ; J.EFarrell and T Wilkinson, half-backs;

H Smith, W Kiddie, J Gandy, J Hardman G Woods, Barber, J Bingham, T Pennington, and Sampson, for- wards. St. Helens: Haseldon, back; M'Nelly, Flesthani and Halton, three-quarter backs; Liptrot and Dearden, half-backs • Finney, Twist, Addison, Holt, Johnson, M‘Loughlin, Basnett, Marsh, and James, forwards. RUNCORN V. Dawsama. The premier Cheshire or- ganisation paid a visit to Dewsbury, on Saturday, to encounter the shoddy team. The visitors were without the ' services of Woods, their full back; but the home team were about the strongest they have turned out this sea- son, including Lockwood and Graham, the latter ap- pearing for the first time since his return from abroad. Wolstenhohne, the home captain, kicked off at three o'clock, Speakman returning to half-way. Runcorn worked the oval into the Dewsbury 25, where Stewart obtained posseasicrn and kicked well into the visitors' quarters, and Hopkins following up the advantage thus gained, got a try, but the place was too difficult for Lockwood to improve upon. After the drop-out Dews- bury again assumed the aggressive, and from a line-out rin Runcorn 25, Weistenholme collared the oval and dashed over the line, Lockwood again failing at gal. Roth these pointa were obtained before the game had I been in progress ten minutes. Speakman dropped out Graham returning into the *visitors' 25, and Runcorn, by a series of short rushes reached the half-way flag, but the leather was gradually worked back again, and from a scrimmage Stadden passed to Lockwood (full back), who drooped a beautiful goal. These reverses stirred up Runcorn, and after Graham had notched a minor fmip an ineffectual shot at goal the visitors got into the Dewsbury 25, where several., tough scrimmages occurred. Kicking between tne respective backs here took place, the ball eventually settling at the centre, while Stadden passed to Graham, who almost scored, being pushed into touch on the goal line. From the line-out Cawley ran finely to half-way. Here Andrews ran well, but a bad pass to Speakman neu- tralized the advantage thus gained, and half-time was announced with the game raging in neutral territory. Runcorn restarted, and after the return scrimmaging commenced in Runcorn quarters, Hopkins passed to Graham, who had hard lines, slipping a yard from the line. The visiting forwards now played well together, and by a concerted dribble invaded their op- ponents' 25, where Davies got the oval, and made a fine run, finishing up with a pass to Speakman, but the tackling was good, and he was held just outside the coveted line. Kicking amongst the home backs removed hostilities to the other end, and Graham picked up and threaded through his opponents, scoring a try in a favourable position, but Jackson failed at goal. div.head: NOTED FOOTBALLER.
div.p: A NOTED FOOTBALLER.

In a recent issue of a Manchester periodical appears a capital lithographed portrait of Mr. Sam Williams, of• Ited Bank, Newton-le-Willows, the noted Rugby foot- baller. Under the heading of " Famous Football Players" the following particulars in reference to Mr. Williams are furnished :—The subject of our portrait this week is Mr. S. Williams, captain of the famous Sal- ford club. Like many other valu4l members of the borough club, his football eddcation commenced with the Crescent, the year 1879 being the first occasion on which he donned a jersey. After the amalgamation of the Salford and Crescent clubs, our subject joined the Swinton F.C., for which he played in the second team part of the season of 1881-82. 'Mere were too many as- sociations connected with his old club to allow him to remain long there; and before the season was over he had found his way back to his old friends, who had en masse joined Salford. Starting with the second team he soou worked his way into the first's ranks, and 1882-83 found him a fixture in the first team, for whom he played three-quarter back. This was Sam's most suc- cessful year, as, in addition to dropping a couple of goods, he scored no less than thirteen tries—a capital /word for one season. His play at this time was very fine, and we well remember seeing him against Bolton at the latter end of the season' his performance on that day being one of the very finest ever seen on any ground. The following year found him captaining the A team, a position which he voluntarily took in order to look after the rising talent; but 1885-88 found him again in the first team, this tiine amongst the forwards, in which position he has played ever since. Last year's perfor- mances are pretty fresh in the memories of footballers, and it is sufficient to say that, having a chance int the county trial game, his play was of such an excellent character that ho was selected for several of the county engagements, and when the North and South match Was decided, Mr. Williams was one of the forwards doing duty for the North—the highest honour that had up to then been conferred upon any member of the Salford F.C. Mr. Variety's retirement from the captaincy of the S.F.C. led to the election of Mr. Williams to the vacant post, and it is no exaggeration to say thee in this position he has given satisfaction to both the members of his own club and to the players and spectators connected with other organisations, his conduct being always that of a gentleman, and of one who plays the game for the game's sake. Like many other footballers, Mr. Williams has taken an interest in amateur sports;' and although he has not shown any grand performances, still he has had a fairly successful career, winning a prize in -nearly every contest in which he has taken part.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The meeting of the old rivals, St. Helens and Widnes clubs, on the ground of the first-named, was an "at- tractive item" in the holiday pleasures of the suppor- ters of the respective organisations. Owing to the bad "form" of the St. Helens men during the past two months the match was considered a "sure thing" for the Widnesians, and such it proved. The St. Helens team had bad luck in not scoring, while .the visitors played a splendid defensive game. On Monday a team of the St. Helens club visited Ossett, and met the latter club on its own ground, a good game resulting in a capital victory for the:visitors.

The premier team of Warrington showed up particu larly well on Saturday and Monday, on which days they met Oldham and Wigan, and defeated in a decisive fas- hion both of these formidable clubs. It is doubtful whether Warrington have at any previous time during this season displayed such no all-round form as they did in these two matches. The dash and combination of the forwards was splendid, and the play of the backs cool and calculated. Among the forwards Ashton par- ticularly distinguished himself on both days by hard work and intelligent passing, but at the same time each and all of the others worked with a will and us.selfishly. At half back Warren's tactics were particularly effec- tive on Monday, but here, too, Speakman was at his best. Of the threequartera It would be unfair to men- tion one before another, but it can safely be said that both Barnes and Jolley never played hater than they did at both matches, whilst Appltton showed wonderful quickness in following up any advantage and in always being to hand when wanted. Judging by his efforts on Saturday and Monday Nevins seemg' to be rapidly developing into a champion full back. On both occasions he displayed that prime requisite for the post—coolness, and when he had anything like a chance he rarely, if ever, failed in clearing his lines. It is not often that football spectators have a nicer treat afforded them than the manner in which theWarrin.- tonians turned the tables oa Wigan on Monday. For the first few minutes it seemed as though all was up with the home team. The leather had Wely been started when Slevin's followers forced it over the. Warrington lines as though there was no one to oppose them, and it had been scarcely kicked out when they again went through the same operation. This challenge to a fast game was, however, quickly taken up by the home team, and after that the Wigan men were fairly overwhelmed by the brilliant play of their opponents. It almost soems that a bad beginning means a good finish for War- rington. To-day the " wiredmwers" will journey to Wakefield to meet the" Trinity" of that town—the crack club of Yorkshire. It would perhaps be too sanguine to expect them to haul down the colours of their opponeaats on their own ground, but if they close the week in the , same form as they began it, they will not be fax be- hind.

The Warrington "I" team suffered its first defeat of the season at Oldham on Saturday. Unfortunately, from one cause and another the team has been a good deal weakened lately,- and on Saturday it was even weaker than usual. But, in spite of this, it was after all more in luck thal in play that they suffered in comparison with their clpponents.

ALLEGED SHOCKING RAILWAY OUTRAGE. • A PRESCOT GENTLEMAN IN CUSTODY. , Early yesterday morning a strong rumour was circulated in St. Helens, Prescot, and district that a well known professional gentleman, residing in the neighbourhood of Prescot. had been apprehended on a serious charge late on Thursday night. It is stated that as the 11-10 p.m train from Liverpool to St. Helens Junction and Manchester was running be- tween Broad Green and Roby, the guard observed a young woman standing on the footboard of one of the carriages. He drew the attention of the driver and the train was brought to a standstill. The girl complained of the conduct of the Prescot gentle- man alluded to, and added that a companion, another young lady, who had been in the same compartment had fallen from the springboard of the train.,whilst it was in motion. She charged the gentleman with having attempted to assault them, and on the arrival of the train' at Huytou the ac- was given into custody.

div.head: STEAMER ON FIRE.
div.p: A STEAMER ON FIRE.
400 LIVES LOST.

With the arrival of the mails from the Far East come particulars of the frightful catastrophe which took place in the Canton river on the 15th ultimo, and was briefly reported at the time by telegraph. The steamer Wah Yeung, from Hong Kong to Can- ton, with about five hundred Chinese passengers, was burned to the water's edge, and four hundred persons lost their lives. The fire broke out about 9 p.m. in the after hold; the ship's 'head was turned to the shore, which was only about two hundred yards distant, and in a few minutes she was beached opposite aChinese fort. The passen- gers who succeeded in reaching the deck had to jump overboard; but a large number were drowned before reaching the shore, and before help could be

given. By far the larger number never reached the deck at all, but were suffocated or burnt below. Among these were about a hundred "small-footed "Chinese women. The Chinese soldiers treated the European officers with the utmost kindness, and rescued them from a crowd of the passengers who threatened to murder them for having, caused the fire. Numbers of Chinese craft were in the vicinity of the burning steamer, but made no efforts to save the drowning passengers; on the contrary, 'the crews plundered everything within their reach. The inquiry into the cause of the accident had not been held when the mail left, but it was be- lieved to be due to the circumstances that the lower deck of the vessel was so deeply saturated with the leakage of kerosene oil—which for several weeks previously had formed the principal part of the cargo—that a spark from an opium smokeeti lamp, or some other fire, ignited the woodwork, and the fire spread so rapidly that it was soon beyond control. In 20 minutes from the first alarm the steamer was burned down to the water's edge.

div.head: LONDON THEATRE DESTROYED.
div.p: A LONDON THEATRE DESTROYED.

; SEVERAL INJURED.—MANY HORSES KILLED. A most disastrous fire broke out early on Thurs- day morning at the Grand Theatre, Islington, Lon- - den, where the pantomime of" Whittington and his cat" had just been launched. Originating at the rear of the theatre, the flames spread with such rapidity that within little more than an hour the building was unroofed and gutted. The fire resul- ted in the total destruction of the building. Dur- ing the evening, and up to half-past eleven, the theatre was crowded with people who had come to witness the Christmas pantomime of "Whittington And his cat." After thekaudience had left, the fire- man (Furlong), going his rounds. diicovered nothing amiss. At about one o'clock, however, he discovereda slight fire on the "gridiron," and im- mediately turned on the hose near the stage. Owing to the inflammable nature of the flies the flames rapidly increased, and the fireman at ono° raised an alarm from the front of the premi'se.s. Two police- , men (Thomas and O'Brien) instantly '+lew „their whistles and alarmed the fire stations. In the front portion of the premises the family of Mr. Wilmot, the lessee, were sleeping, and the constables pro- ceeded to rescue them. Happily, they found a ladder near the pay-box, and succeeded, with the assistance ef Dr. Ross and Mr. Golding, both of 1 Upper-street, in bringing down in safety the whole of the occupants—namely, Mrs. Wilmot and .an elderly lady, and three children, the latter being rescued by Dr. Ross. Mr. Wilmot himself had not retired to rest. By the time the work of rescue .had been accomplished the flames had secured a, hold on the building, and fire-engines from all parts' of the metropolis, under the personal direction of Captain Shaw, poured on volumes of water until all the neighbouring thoroughfarbe were flooded, but all efforts were unavailing, and by half- past one the roof 0f,,, the .• building fell in, and nothing could .be one but to keep the flames from spreading to the adjoining. premises. The actors and actresses have lost all their stage property, and some of them their private ward- robes; and it is estimated that quite 300 persons Iwill be thrown out of employment. Mr. Wilmot, the proprietor, states that the total loss approaches £20,000. The building was insured, but the value of the contents is not covered. The pantomime, "Whittington and his Cat," proved a decided success when produced on Monday night. There were 300 performers of various grades, and the cost of putting it on the stage is stated to have been £6,000. Last night some 3,500 persons' visited the theatre, and money had to be returned. The house was cleared by twenty minutes past eleven. The electric light was extinguished, leav- ing only a few gas jets remaining for the conven- ience of the employes. . .... _ i —.

Eleven horses- ere killed and their attendants seriously injured owing to the northern gable of the theatre falling upon a stable. Seven persons in all were on the premises when the fire broke out, but all were rescued in safety. One man, named Henry Fairelougb, was severely injured during the fire and taken to the hospital. '

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER
LONDON. THURSDAY NIGOLY.

A fortnight hence, on the 13th of January, ii will be just thirteen years since Mr. Gladstone wrote his famous letter to "My dear Granville," dated from Carlton House Terrace. "At the age of sixty-Ave," he said, "and after forty-two years of laborious pub- lic life, I think myself entitled to retire on; the present opportunity. This retirement is dictated to me by my personal views as to the best method of spending the closing years of my life." A great deal has happened since the 13th of January, 1875. Boys and girls at scbool when it was written have grown into men and women. Middle-aged men have be- gun to think it is time for them to retire, and many fantails men of the day, not forgetting Mr. Disraeli, have passed away for ever. Yet here is Mr. Glad- stone posting night and day on the long journey to Florence. his projected rest being significantly- de- signed with the object of husbanding his strength for a final effort, perhaps the most momentous, cer- tainly the most difficult, of his life. Younger men would have been content to quietly set out on the journey with such preliminary husbanding of strength as it seems to require. Mr. Gladstone, travelling through a snowstorm, delivered an im- portant and lengthy speech by way of preface to his journey in December weather across the Channel. _ .

These evidences of mental and physical vitality, phenomenal in themselves, are well calculated to have a depressing effect in the councils of the Con- servative party. It seems quite years ago that some of the franker spoken among them openly avowed their hope that "Old Gladstone was played out," , and that the time of deliverance was at hand. Some of them in the House of Commons, prominent among them being Lord Randolph Churchill and our newly-appointed Minister to the Shah, en- deavoured to hasten this conclusion by worrying the veteran statesman. To work him up into an uncontrollable passion, to add to his herculean. labours of the day the meaner worries of a p longed night's wrangle, seemed to be worth all t;- trouble it cost them, since it seemed a certain way of breaking down Mr Gladstone's health. Only those in constant attendance at the House ' of Commons can realise the kind of badgering Mr. Gladstone has been subjected to through the long years since he announced to "My dear Granville" his intention of retiring. The climax was reached one night in the spring of 1878, when Mr. Gladstone issuing from the "No" lobby, where he had been voting against some proposal of the Government, was suddenly set upon by a mob of some fort's, or fifty English gentlemen, who howled and groaned at him, some, in their mad frenzy, even shaking their fists at him. Mr. Gladstone paused a moment, startled by the sudden cry, then, crossing the space that divides the two lobbies, he stood for a few mo- ments calmly surveying through the glass door the yelling mob, whose cries were redoubled. It was a memorable scene, which I dare say the majority of those who took part in it would be glad to forget. It was worse than usual, but was a fair, if striking, illustration of the treatment to which Mr. Gladstone was nightly subjected by the majority of the House of Commons, where Jingo was king, and Disraeli his prophet. Mr. Gladstone has in the present Par- liament occasionally stiff times. But there is nothing like the vicious spirit that manifested itself in the Parliament of 1874 or that of 1880, in which his Conservative revilers were actively and cordially assisted by the Irish members, who are now among his loudest adulators. He has lived through all these varying scenes and stages, and, what depresses the Tories, is the conviction that he means to live until he has carried Home Rule for Ireland. That his life and strength will be prolonged and maintained for the period necessary for this work, Mr. Gladstone himself is perfectly sure. At the same time, whilst he trusts in Providence, he takes infinite care of himself. On his way to Dover, on 'Tuesday, people were astonished and alarmed to see him standing bareheaded in the snowstorm, and he was earnestly entreated to put on his hat. It • seems a dangerous thing for anyone to do, espe- • cially one on the verge of eighty. But Mr. Glad- stone knows what he is about, and is aware that he is impregnable to cold in the matter of a bared head. I remember eight years ago, daring the first Midlothian campaign, he spoke at a northern rail- - way-station for more than ten minutes bareheaded, -with the snow thickly falling. Speaking to him in the evening on the subject, he told me that, except for appearance, he could safely walk bareheaded through the streets in all weathers. At work with his axe, in the seclusion of Hawarden, he rarely wears hat or cap. Be sure, if he ran any risk, he would not uncover his head when speaking out of doors. He has to live to see Home Rule granted to 'lrelahl, and would not for any momentary gratifl- - imperil his chances. The principal lion in Mr. Jiladstone's y.ath is the lirrobability that the present Conservative Govern- ment will anticipate him, and after denouncing the advocates of Home Rule as traitorous, will concede Home Rule themselves. As this correspondence testifies, that is an opinion I have always held, and it is certainly strengthened by the remarkable action just taken by the Irish Government. Avail- ing themselves of a section of the Land Law Act for the current year, they have, at a single blow, reduced the judicial rents of Ireland by an amount estimated in some quarters to reach a higher figure than the aggregate deductions made by the sub- commissioners and by agreements between landlord and tenants since the passing of the Land Act of 1885. This is really a magnificent, not to say theatrical, throwing up of the sponge. It is a whole- sale surrender to the National party, a sudden movement to march in harmony with the Plan of Campaign. It is a curious irony of fate that, whilst, Mr. O'Brien and the Lord Mayor of Dublin are in prison for urgieg the necessity of a reduction of the judicial rent, Mr. Balfour, _at liberty and in office, takes council with his eollevues, and by a stroke of the pen does more in the way of redacing the income of the landlords •than the Land League has been able to accomp- lish since the date of its institution. It need hardly be said that this ',need are on the part of the Government, the force of which has been dramatically increased by the suddenness and unexpectedness of the blow, has almost stunned the landlord party. If Mr. Glad- stone had done it they would have understood. But that their own familiar friends, their boasted champion, should thus assail them piles agony on agony. The worst of the situation, regarded from a Ministerial point of view, is that in estranging their own friends they have not succeeded in en- listing the goodwill of the adversary. They have gone a long step in the direction taken by the Land Leaguers, but they have not gone far enough. They have admitted the whole principle for the advocacy of which Mr. O'Brien is now sleeping on a plank' bed. But they have fallen short of the practical 'effect necessitated by the actual state of affairs. Her Majesty's Ministers are Land Leaguets. But whilst they have gone a great deal too far for the landlords, tliey have not gone far enough for the tenants. In 'lassie they appear to be taking Lord Randolph Churchill serious] y,and are now alone in that attitude. Even the Berlin and Vienna newspapers, which at the outset of the journey began to think.there was something in it. have discovered the mistake and dropped the noble lord into ignominious oblivion. In London his latest peregrination is regarded with perhaps just a lingering spark of admiration for this -rresh development of his superlative "cheek." Of mrse, Lord Randolph as a private individual is at rty to spend his recess where and how he 7ps. But as a public man, who has been a ter of the Crown and may he one again, his trumpeted visit to Berlin and St. Peters- regarded a., ebullitions of sheer impudence. have Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett next leaving
his card on Prince Bismarck, and hoping he does not intrude when. he pokes his head into tne Czar's private room at Gatsch;na.

A paper contributed to " Galignani's Messenger" by Miss Emily Faithful has called attention to the endeavours made by some ladies of good position: but reduced income, to earn their own living. There is a bric-a-brac shop just opened in Davies-street, Berkeley-square, by two well-known ladies. Whilst reference is made to this, and to Miss Robinson's en- terprising career in Manchester as a saleswoman of artistic work and house decoration, I have not seen any reference to pioneers in this work who have been established to my personal knowledge for over ten years. These are the Misses Garratt, sisters of Mrs. _Fawcett, and of that prosperous medical practitioner, Dr. liarmtt Anderson. Mrs. Anderson has a wide and growing practice, of course exclusively among ladies, and receives her guinea fee for a few moments' con- sultation, with the best of male doctors. Even be- fore she made a nante for herself, her sisters had formed a good business in the way of house decnra- tion. There are many people who like to live in pretty houses, and do not knovr bow to create them. Two such, whom I happen to know, living in widely separated districts of Lorxfou, some years ago placed their houses in the charge of the Misses Gas. ratt, and within a certain, rough arid liberal estimare; gave them carte blatterir to furnish it according to their own tastes. ?he Misses Garrett charge commission on their work, and indigo course present a tastefully furnished residence todhe happy house- holder. ?or ladies Yehere the taste, this is, 11 have reason to believe..envich better business than shirt making, or tIYBEI, the creation of button- holes. The Wilson seandal bandied away in Paris.now. the object of the conspirators being-attained and 3i3.- Gr 43, dismissed. One other reason why the up- roar against M. Wilson. should cettes,is that every man who kiows anything- of political life in Paris knows that it is no new thing for decorations to bin trafficked in I hear of a curious instance front one involuntarily concerned in tle transaction' He is an wells-known manufactwer who hashi business relations with a French firm. One. day, towels-N. the close of the last Paris exhibition, he cashed an, order drown upon hinst by his Paris correspondent for .£1,290,. Sometimeafter, meeting the Frenchnian, the lattertold him that this money was required literally to purchase the. Legion (if Honour, which he had received in connection with the exhibition of a particular manulacture. These was no secrecy about the matter. Ha-had arranged the purchase and paid the money as if it were for so many tons of copper or bushels of wheat. That, of course,, was in the palmy days .of the Empire. But, as we know, the stricter virtue of the Republic is not proof against temptation.

THE SHIP CANAL SCHESTE.

Sir,—lt has been said that "history repeats itself," and, as I have listened to a good deal that has been st,tid about the Ship Canal scheme, and watched the eppo.ti- tion to which it has been subjected by interested parties, I have been strongly reminded of thi . opposition to the making of the Duke of Bridgewater' s Canal. For in- Fiance we read :—" The Old Quay Navigation, even at the last moment, thought to delay, if not to defeat, the Duke's operations, by lowering their rates nearly one- half. Only a few days after the royal assent had been given to the bill, they published an announcement, ap- propriateclly dated the Ist of April, setting forth the large sacrifice they were about to make, and intimating that from their reductions in carriage a real and per- manent advantage will arise to the public, and they will experience that utility so cried up of late, but which has hitherto only existed in promises. The Duke heeded not the ineffective blow thus aimed at him; he wail or'y more than ever resolved to go forward with his Canal."— Yours, Icc.,

div.head: "ALDERMAN CROSFIELD AND MR. JOHN WHITE."
div.p: "ALDERMAN CROSFIELD AND MR. JOHN WHITE."

Sir,—lt seems that Mr. Crosfield was entirely mis- taken when he assumed that Mr. John White was like other men. Most of the people who display any activity in advocating "Fair Trade, ' make little attempt to con- ceal their expectations that a change of fiacal policy will put money 'n their pockets, but Mr. John Wnite, it seems, is of an ethereal comp -isition and not at all sus- ceptible to these grosser influences. Roughly speaking, those who have a leaning towards Fair Trade may be put under the three class of landlords, tenant farmers, and working-men, The landlord thinks that Fair Trade would prevent the rent of his land from falling, the ten- ant farmer believes that it would raise the price of his produce, and the workman who has been smitten with the economic heresy has a vague feeling that an imposi- tion of duties on imports would 'give him more regular employment, and perhaps raise his wages. In each and every case it is the expectation of pecuniary benefit that prompts the Fair Trade cry. But Mr. John White re- pudiates with scorn the suggestion that he is as other Fair Traders are. Like the Pharisee in the temple he will have nothing to do with common-place publicans and sinners. He stands in the high altitudes of a pure, but ostentatious philanthropy. A Riettiy regarded, there is nothing that Fair Traders need be much ashamed of in admitting that self-interest lies at the root of their a titation. Nearly all political, and especially economical, movements have been prompted by a more or less enffghtened self-interest. The free trade agitation of nearly half a century ago is often referred to as affording an instance of great public spirit in those who carried it oe, yet even the free traders we e not entirely disinterested. The big manu- facturers who took a leadiir part in the agitation had got hold of the doctrines of Adam Smith and other economists that, when the necessaries of life were cheap, the wages of labour were low, and they very naturally came to the conclusion that if they could reduce the price of coni by abolishing the corn laws they would be able to get cheaper Tabour, and by getting cheaper labour manufacture cheaper goods, with the result that the output of their factories would be increased. So that even the free trade movement was very- largely a ' contest between manufacturers who wished to, p4t money into their pockets and landowners who wished to , keep what they had in theirs. Of course, motives of this sort were not unnecessarily paraded by the free traders any more than they are to-day by the fair r traders, but most people know that politicians and ai- tators generally have two sets of renson.s for their actions—one set for public consumption and the other r for private inspiration.—/ am, sir, • SCEPTIC- Warrington, December, 1887.

div.head: LIQUOR TRAFFIC.
div.p: THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC.

Sir,—l have been much pleased in reading in your last issue the letter of our friend, • Mr. Butler, on "The National Prohibitive Party." Like many more Christian men, no doubt, his grieve(' feelings have been somewhat pent up; but here he bursts out at last through the organ. of the Press, and condemns the liquor traffic as an. "em brutalising and pauperising trade." It is very ratify- in g to temperance workers to see from time to time the principles of temperance brought to the front in your weekly issue, and also the prominent position taken up by the" Examiner" itself in this peat reform. It may seem to be, and is, the same ground that has been trod by many of our fellows when Mr. B. says that "it is the fruitful source of crime, insanity, pauperism, and untold misery; " but still the statements remain true; and lam inclined to think that by the constant repetition of the words and the everyday knowled„onand sight of the facts themselves, we are too apt to lose sight of their vast weight and importance. Surely there is no one who has witnessed a tine intelligent workman succumb to such a misfortune Ls that of intemperance, which may have led him to insanity, suicide, or crime, but what has felt downright sorry. It is an irreparable lose to lose one's reasoning power, and yet it is true that many have and are losing it, either temporarily or per- manently. There is nothing whatever inviting about poverty and ruin both of constitution, and all future; prospects of happiness, and yet this is the position that the liquor traffic has brought many thousands of men and women to. What can be done, it might be asked, that has not al- ready been done, in order that these things might be abolished? Again and again there have been appeals made to Parliament, both by prominent members of the House and by many petitions from the people. Many have been the efforts that have been put forthlay the United Kingdom Alliance, and the endeavours of the national prohibitive party, the objects of which, "to secure the suppression of the liquor traffic by the direct and drastic remedy of imperial enactment," arena to be overlooked: but still our efforts have been largely and almost coldly disregarded. We have begged and prayed them to close the public-houses on the Lord's day • but even the sanctity of that day has been laid aside—only barely acknowledging it by closing them for a few hours. You well remember only a few months ago how the people of Durham were treated when they made applicationfor it for their own county ? A large majority of their repre- sentatives were in favour of that bill (a fact sufficient in itself to prove the mind of the people). and accordingly it was brought into the House of Commons and passed right through to the "House of the Refiners "—the House of Lords, and even there passel the second read- ing ; but. when it came to the third, Lord Salisbury said, coldly enough, "that he did not think the people were ready for it. Lord Salisbury doesn't know the pain that those words sent to the hearts of righteous men neither is he aware of the disappointment they caused among the people of Durham, especially when they saw that it was also rejected. And this coldness has not only been manifest, Mr. Editor, among the Conservative party of that house; it tins even strikingly. been, marked in our friend, Mr. Gladstone. But more of this in my next letter.—Yours, JOS. ELLISON. I Latchford, December 29th, 1887.

div.head: SOIREE' AT CHESTER.
div.p: SOIREE' AT CHESTER.

A soiree in connection with Mr. Gladstone's birth- dayrpromoted bathe Chester, Liberal Association. was herd on Wednesday night, at the Town Hall, and attended by several thousand people. Mr. Deeley, flesidentt of the Association, occupied the chair. Sir Walter Faster.. M.P., congratulated his old friends in Cheat-et-upon the fact that every time he had come- to Chester d'aring the last twelve months it had been apparent to him that Chester Liberal- ism was growing stronger and stronger, and it was never more robust and determined than it was at this moment, never more devoted to the great prin- ciples of freeeont and' justice. (Cheers.) The name of one man had beep growing in their affection, as it had been grewingin. that of the people generally, the name of Mr, GladAtone—(loud th.,..s)—and he was glad that ChesterliberaLahati wished him "God speed " on his journey to obtain a well-won rest. (Cheers.) No leader orthe-peoplac had ever been so gretted by the people on his way through the land, and in every poor man' cabin in- Deland the people prayed that God might bless the "Grand Old Man' who had sent a ray of hope into the.aptb of Ireland's despair. and told the Irish people, with; wonderful and prophetic insight, that the heart of the Ehglish democracy was full of sym- pathy and' ove toward a the poor peasantry of -Ireland. .(Cheers.) It was that message of peace and good-will which-was alone likely to put an' end to crime and out-, rage; and'to makoverice and happiness Possible between the two peoples: That was the true message of the people of Einglandto the people of' Ireland—a Christmas message. of'peare and'good:orill: (Cheers.) litunner, who was received with cheers, referred to the remark-made.by the Doctor to the effect that he always came-to-Chester for rest and refreshment. So did he (the speaker); and he always got a very good dinner. (Laughter.)' He was aivrara very much plea.sed to come to Chester,. because he had got the notion that they were such a ibily good-humoured lot. (Laughter.) ' That was characteristic. of their whole party, for no matter how-often they. were knocked down they never knew when they were beaten. (Applause.) Let them ' compare the speeches delivered on the Liberal side with those made by maeLord Hartington, Mr. Goschen, and Lord' Randolph. (Groans.) Their speeches were as hitter as- gall: (Laughter.) Twelve months ago thee LiberaLsavere- sroashed and utterly pulverized ; but it. - was true they were popping, up again. kLaughter.) Lot them campare tbe speeches on the other side with those.. of 'Lord' Rosebery; who was always ready ith a joker Sir William. Ihevourt, who was full of irony and fun— (aPoplause)'—and' with the speeches given by Mr. Jot* Morley. (applause.) The Tatter did not contain maw- jokes, but therwero always foil of commonsense and of'. the spirit of kindness. That was the spirit whilth, ' animated Liberal's—let them keep that spirit and Clay'' would only need the chance to do as Northwich (Applause.) Yea, he was told that Mr. Yarburghwas 'about to be. married. ("Oh," and laughter.) He did not wonder at them laughing—he (Mr. Brunnerjahad 'seen hint. (Iteneyredlauehter.)- He wondered whather hia tadv had ever nand any of his speeches. He faticied not. Redid not think any girl who had read thetravould be so anxious to have him. (Laughter.) Mr. Yeakitmgh had recently- put credit upon himself by slanderiag: him (the sneaker). He was a very small person ccsaitatred with afr. Yerburgh, and he thought Mr. Yerburattobould let him alline. (Laughter.) When a man got rairriedhe generally- made a new will. He thought it was right that when that event happened young-men shoeld turn over new-leaf. and he would like Mr: Yerburgh tiresign for Cheater and give them the chariot) of doing a. ntiaa thing. (Laughter and applause.) - M. Herbert Gladstone, M.A...waa called tom for a speech, and said they could Rot help remembering that last June there was a slight accident in Chiaster—(laugh- ! ter)--are accident to the turgoof 80 votes otr so; but he ; hoped they would bear in rftiml that whem the next op- portunitv came, there mutt be no accidens of any kind., (Cheers.) He thought Val-might fairly-ask the sturdy- Liberals of Chester to be trite to their principles, andthaw they might be trusted not to be led a-ow by social intaa- eneea, however powerfler and enticing,. ('Hear, hear.) The year which was about to close had netbeen a very p2t.as- ' int! year for many of them. As Sir Walter Foster aad said, they had had a groat deal of hard political -work to clo.tnit he hoped that they had sown good SINN& and that in the new Year, which wets about to davit, we should see good fruit produced.. There was gttiorn in many gfirections, They could not help having Hot know- ledge that hero in England there was a gulf between them and their old friends, whioh was daily widening; and in Ireland we saw the gloom at present deepening. They saw that it required all the help moderate men could !aloe to keep the people quiet, and to make them abstain from the violence to which they were provoked by the action of the Government. They could only hope most earnestly that the coming. year would bring about a better state of things both in England and Ireland, awl he appealed to the LibotALl
